hidden_passages.what: False-positive substring matches: 'pension' inside 'suspension'/'suspensions', and 'PERS' inside words like 'personnel', 'papers', 'supersede', etc. Not pension-related content.

hidden_poi: A $6,007,000 appropriation for 'pension system modernization' at the Department of Retirement Systems is funded through this supplemental operating budget rather than through any pension-titled bill; it is a real, multi-million-dollar IT modernization project for retirement system administration.

This bill functions as the fiscal enabling vehicle for several substantive pension bills passed the same session: SB 5676 (PERS/TRS Plan 1 benefit increase), HB 1669 (PSERS disability benefits), SB 5367 (inactive retirement accounts), and HB 1752 (Roth option in the deferred compensation program). Funding for each is explicitly contingent on the companion bill's enactment by June 30, 2022, with a lapse clause if it fails - a common budget-bill technique for making substantive policy changes contingent on appropriation.

None of this rises to the level of amending core pension RCWs (PERS/TRS/SERS/PSERS/LEOFF chapters) directly - HB 1141 itself doesn't set contribution rates or benefit formulas - but it is the money that makes those contingent pension bills operative, which is exactly the kind of hidden pension-adjacent content an RCW-classification-only screen would miss.

No sign of contribution-rate suspensions or actuarial funding-method changes in this bill; the actuarial references found are all health-insurance/Medicaid rate-setting, not pension funding actuarial work.

The bulk of raw term matches (pension, PERS, SERS, TRS, PSERS) were substring false positives (suspension, personnel, papers, supersede, etc.) and should be filtered out of any automated RCW/pension-term classifier to avoid inflating apparent pension-relatedness.

brief: Defining attending provider and clarifying other provider functions for workers' compensation claims, and adding psychologists as attending providers for mental health only claims.
triage_how: This bill does not affect public retirement systems; it amends workers' compensation law to define attending provider roles and add psychologists as providers for mental health claims only.

brief: Concerning actuarial funding of state retirement systems.
haiku_summary: The bill temporarily eliminates employer minimum contribution requirements for amortizing unfunded actuarial accrued liabilities in Plan 1 of PERS, TRS, SERS, and PSERS by instituting 0% contribution rates from 2024 through 2029.

deep_provisions.detail: Amends RCW 41.45.060(6)(b), (7)(b), and (8)(b) to replace "subject to any minimum or maximum rates applied pursuant to" with "unless superseded by" RCW 41.45.150, conforming the PERS/PSERS and TRS employer UAAL-amortization formula to the new 0% supersession provisions added to .150.

Strikes "or maximum" from the "minimum or maximum rates" reference in RCW 41.45.060(6)(c), (7)(c), and (8)(c), removing the maximum-rate qualifier that had bounded benefit-improvement amortization surcharges collected in addition to RCW 41.45.150 rates.

Amends RCW 41.45.150(4) to add a fixed sunset of June 30, 2025 to the 3.50% minimum PERS/PSERS employer contribution for PERS 1 UAAL amortization, striking the prior open-ended condition that it remain effective "until the actuarial value of assets... equals one hundred percent of the actuarial accrued liability."
Amends RCW 41.45.150(5) to add a fixed sunset of August 31, 2025 to the 3.50% minimum SERS employer contribution for PERS 1 UAAL amortization, striking the same open-ended 100%-funded condition.
Amends RCW 41.45.150(6) to add a fixed sunset of August 31, 2024 to the 5.75% minimum TRS employer contribution for TRS 1 UAAL amortization, striking the same open-ended 100%-funded condition.
Adds new RCW 41.45.150(7) establishing a 0% contribution rate that supersedes the PERS/PSERS employer UAAL-amortization rate from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2029.
Adds new RCW 41.45.150(8) establishing a 0% contribution rate that supersedes the SERS employer UAAL-amortization rate from September 1, 2025 through August 31, 2029.

Adds new RCW 41.45.150(9) establishing a 0% contribution rate that supersedes the TRS employer UAAL-amortization rate from September 1, 2024 through August 31, 2029, a window that opens before the bill's own effective date of any later action and roughly a year ahead of the parallel PERS/SERS holidays.

Amends renumbered RCW 41.45.150(10) to direct the state actuary to review the appropriateness of "establishing, removing, or adjusting" minimum contribution rates (previously limited to reviewing existing minimum rates), broadening the recurring biennial review mandate.
Repeals uncodified 2021 c 334 s 747, a 2021 session-law provision whose substance is not reproduced in this bill's text.

deep_whoAffected: Public employers in PERS, SERS, PSERS, and TRS (state agencies, local governments, school districts, and by extension PERS 1/TRS 1 retirees whose plans depend on continued UAAL funding)
deep_poi: Converts an open-ended minimum-contribution floor tied to reaching 100% funded status into a fixed-term floor followed by a four-year 0% rate holiday for PERS 1/TRS 1 UAAL amortization -- a shift from funded-status-driven policy to calendar-driven policy, decoupling employer contribution relief from actual plan funding levels.

The TRS 0% holiday (RCW 41.45.150(9)) opens September 1, 2024, roughly a year ahead of the parallel PERS/PSERS holiday (July 1, 2025) and SERS holiday (September 1, 2025) -- an asymmetric schedule across systems sharing the same PERS 1/TRS 1 legacy liability that an analyst would want reconciled against each system's funded ratio.

Section 3 repeals a 2021 uncodified operating-budget proviso (2021 c 334 s 747) without stating its content anywhere in the bill -- typical of budget-conforming pension bills but it means the repealed policy can't be assessed from this text alone.

Section 1 quietly strips the "maximum" rate concept from the benefit-improvement amortization surcharge language in RCW 41.45.060(6)(c)/(7)(c)/(8)(c), leaving only an unbounded reference to RCW 41.45.150 rates -- a small drafting change that removes a prior cap concept and could matter if a future plan 1 benefit improvement's surcharge is no longer bounded by a maximum rate.
deep_oneLine: HB 1201 amends RCW 41.45.060 and 41.45.150 to put fixed sunset dates on the existing minimum employer contribution rates that amortize the PERS 1 and TRS 1 unfunded liability, and layers on new four-year 0% supersession windows (TRS starting Sept. 2024, PERS/PSERS/SERS starting mid-2025, all running through 2029), converting an open-ended "until 100% funded" contribution floor into a scheduled, time-limited one.

hidden_how: Grepped for pension-related terms in the bill text, found all 24 occurrences fall within two near-identical copies (effective-date variants) of the RCW 43.84.092 treasury income account earnings-distribution list, which the bill amends only to strike three unrelated accounts (public health services account, state higher education construction account, higher education construction account).

hidden_passages.where: Lines 20-28 (Sec. 3, amending RCW 43.84.092, "Effective until July 1, 2024" version) and lines ~171-179 (parallel post-7/1/2024 version of the same section)
hidden_passages.what: A single very long sentence lists ~150 state accounts and funds entitled to their proportionate share of investment earnings on the treasury pool. Roughly two dozen of the listed accounts are retirement/pension-named (department of retirement systems expense account, judges' retirement account, judicial retirement administrative/principal accounts, PERS plan 1 account, PERS combined plan 2/3 account, pension funding stabilization account, supplemental pension account, TRS plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, Washington judicial retirement system account, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, public safety employees' plan 2 retirement account, school employees' retirement system combined plan 2/3 account, Washington state patrol retirement account, deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts, money-purchase retirement savings administrative/principal accounts, volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund). All of these are simply named as recipients of interest earnings under the existing, unchanged distribution formula.

hidden_passages.where: Same passage, marked with <TextRun amendingStyle="strike">
hidden_passages.what: The bill's only edit to this list is to strike three items: 'the public health services account, the state higher education construction account, the higher education construction account' — consistent with Sections 1-2 of the bill repealing/decodifying those RCW sections. No retirement or pension account is added, struck, or otherwise modified in either copy of the list.

hidden_poi: The bill's actual substance (Sections 1-2) repeals or decodifies seven unrelated dormant accounts (reinvesting in youth account, public health services account, state/higher education construction accounts, fisheries capital projects account, water quality capital account, stadium and exhibition center construction account) and none are pension-related.

Section 3 amends RCW 43.84.092 (and its post-7/1/2024 successor provision) purely to remove the three struck account names from the earnings-distribution roster; the pension/retirement account names are boilerplate carryover text unaffected by the amendment.

No contribution rates, benefit formulas, actuarial assumptions, or funding mechanisms for PERS, TRS, LEOFF, WSPRS, or JRS are touched; the 24 hits are simply proper-noun account names appearing in a routine investment-earnings-allocation list.

The duplicate ~150-account list appears twice in the file because RCW 43.84.092 has two effective-date versions (pre- and post-July 1, 2024) in current law, both of which needed conforming amendments to strike the same three account names.

hidden_how: Grepped the bill text for pension-related terms, found all 24 occurrences fall on exactly two lines (101 and 247), read those lines and their surrounding sections in full to confirm the passages are unedited boilerplate account-name lists within a treasury-interest-allocation statute.

hidden_passages.where: Sec. 9 (amending RCW 43.84.092, "Effective until July 1, 2024" version), subsection (4)(a), line 101
hidden_passages.what: A long, unedited list of state accounts and funds that receive a pro-rata share of state treasury investment earnings (rather than having those earnings swept to the general fund). About a dozen pension-related accounts appear in this list purely as account names: department of retirement systems expense account, deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts, judges' retirement account, judicial retirement administrative/principal accounts, pension funding stabilization account, PERS plan 1 account, PERS combined plan 2/3 account, supplemental pension account, TRS plan 1 account, TRS combined plan 2/3 account, volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, Washington judicial retirement system account, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, WA public safety employees' plan 2 retirement account, SERS combined plan 2/3 account, WA state patrol retirement account, and the higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund. None of these entries is added, removed, or otherwise modified by this bill; the only tracked edits in this paragraph (amendingStyle="add") insert two unrelated new accounts (opioid abatement settlement account, state hazard mitigation revolving loan account).

hidden_passages.where: Sec. 10 (amending RCW 43.84.092, "Effective July 1, 2024" version), subsection (4)(a), line 247
hidden_passages.what: Exact duplicate of the Sec. 9 passage above — WA statute carries two parallel versions of this section (pre- and post-July 2024), both reenacted by this bill with the identical unedited list of pension-related accounts and the same two unrelated additions.

hidden_poi: All 24 pension-term hits are confined to two lines (101 and 247) of the XML — not scattered through the bill — because RCW 43.84.092 exists in two nearly-identical statutory versions (pre/post July 1, 2024) that the bill reenacts in parallel via Sec. 9 and Sec. 10.

This is RCW 43.84.092, the treasury income account statute governing which state accounts share in investment earnings on state treasury surplus balances versus having those earnings swept to the general fund. Pension trust accounts (PERS, TRS, LEOFF, judicial retirement, deferred comp, etc.) are named because they are treasury accounts entitled to their own investment earnings — this is routine, decades-old boilerplate, not new policy.

The bill's only tracked edits within this long account list are additions of two unrelated accounts (opioid abatement settlement account; state hazard mitigation revolving loan account) — no pension account is added, deleted, or reclassified, no contribution rate or benefit is touched, and no actuarial or funding provision appears anywhere in the bill.

This is a clean negative finding: despite 24 raw term hits, there is no hidden pension policy, no contribution-rate suspension, and no proviso affecting retirement funding in ESHB 1203. It is a false positive for pension classification driven entirely by the recurring long account-name list, not substantive content.

hidden_how: Grepped the full bill text for pension/retirement/LEOFF/PERS/actuarial terms and read every hit in context; all 21 occurrences are substring false matches ("pension" inside "suspension/suspending/suspended", "pers" inside "person/persons"), not references to any retirement system.

hidden_passages.where: Lines 13, 89 ("pers" hits)
hidden_passages.what: Substring match of "pers" inside the words "person" ("designate one person") and "persons" — no relation to PERS (Public Employees' Retirement System) or any pension body.

Every instance is a substring match of "pension" embedded within "suspension," "suspending," or "suspended" — terms used throughout the bill's school-discipline provisions (short-term/long-term suspension, emergency expulsion/removal, discretionary discipline). None reference a pension, retirement benefit, contribution, or fund.

hidden_poi: All 21 'pension-related term' hits are false-positive substring matches within 'suspension/suspending/suspended' and 'person/persons' — a keyword-search artifact, not a substantive signal.

The bill's actual substance is entirely education/discipline policy: renaming 'emergency expulsion' to 'emergency removal', requiring model handbook language on harassment/discrimination policies, designating a school district primary contact for nondiscrimination compliance, and student discipline data disaggregation requirements.

No amendments touch Title 41 RCW (retirement systems), no LEOFF/PERS/TRS/SERS references, no actuarial or DRS (Department of Retirement Systems) provisions, and no appropriations or fiscal note language relating to pension funding appears in the bill text.

This is a good illustration of why raw keyword counts on bill text can overstate apparent pension relevance for classification purposes; analysts should disambiguate 'pension' substring hits from whole-word matches before flagging a bill for hidden pension policy.

brief: Ensuring that firefighters who accept promotional firefighter positions within a fire department remain members of the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system.
haiku_summary: The bill clarifies that firefighters promoted to positions requiring experienced firefighter status remain members of the Law Enforcement Officers' and Firefighters' Retirement System.

deep_provisions.detail: Inserts new RCW 41.26.030(17)(d), defining as a statutory "firefighter" any person serving full-time and fully compensated as an employee of a fire department in a position that requires an experienced firefighter, which keeps firefighters who accept promotional positions within LEOFF membership (plan 1 and plan 2 alike, since this new clause is not excluded from plan 2 the way several adjoining clauses are).

Relabels the existing firefighter-definition subsections (17)(d) through (h) as (e) through (i) to make room for the newly inserted (17)(d), a pure renumbering with no substantive change to those clauses' content.

Updates the internal cross-reference in the EMT-firefighter clause from RCW 18.73.030(12) to RCW 18.73.030(13), conforming to the renumbering already made by 2022 c 136 and flagged in the reviser's note; unrelated to the bill's stated policy purpose.

deep_whoAffected: Firefighters who accept promotional (non-civil-service-exam) positions within a fire department; no member class loses eligibility
deep_poi: The operative new language, "a position that requires an experienced firefighter," is undefined and untethered to civil service rank or job title, unlike every other clause in the (17) list, which invites administrative line-drawing by the Department of Retirement Systems over which promotional titles qualify and creates coverage-creep risk over time.

The new clause is not carved out of plan 2 the way the executive-secretary clauses in (17)(e)-(f) are, so it extends to both plan 1 and plan 2 members; keeping promoted staff in LEOFF rather than letting them fall to PERS preserves the employer's LEOFF 2 contribution obligation (a state-shared, statutorily set rate) rather than shifting cost to a different plan and rate structure.

The bill is a single-section, single-RCW-cite fix with no fiscal apparatus: no emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation language, and no retroactivity or contingent effective date, suggesting the drafters read this as closing a definitional gap rather than creating new liability.

A second, unrelated technical correction (updating an EMT cross-reference from RCW 18.73.030(12) to (13)) is bundled into the same already-amended section rather than left for a separate reviser's bill, a minor drafting economy rather than a substantive add.
deep_oneLine: HB 1279 amends the LEOFF definition of "firefighter" in RCW 41.26.030 to add a catch-all for full-time fire department employees in promotional positions requiring an experienced firefighter, so that firefighters who are promoted (e.g., to officer ranks not covered by the existing civil-service-exam or supervisory clauses) remain LEOFF members rather than falling out into PERS or another system.

brief: Concerning environmental, social, and governance reporting and self-directed investment options at the Washington state investment board.
haiku_summary: The bill requires the Washington State Investment Board to offer at least three environmental, social, and governance-aligned self-directed investment options and to report on climate-related financial risks and ESG policies in its portfolios.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 43.33A RCW requiring WSIB to publicly report by January 1, 2024, and every three years thereafter, on its analysis of climate-related financial risk, social responsibility, and proxy voting/corporate governance policy and use, across its private and public market portfolios, including alignment with the Paris climate agreement and the state climate commitment act.

Defines "climate-related financial risk" to include physical risks (storms, sea level rise, temperature) and transition risks (carbon emission costs, policy shifts, changing economics of carbon-intensive industries) for purposes of the new reporting mandate.

Reenacts and amends RCW 43.33A.190 to require that, beginning January 1, 2024, WSIB provide no fewer than three self-directed investment options consistent with the ESG policies examined under the new reporting section, reflecting a range of ESG-related policy preferences and investment objectives to the extent consistent with fiduciary duty.

deep_whoAffected: Self-directed (defined contribution) account holders only: TRS plan 3, SERS plan 3, and PERS plan 3 members, plus WA ABLE program and (if selected) DreamAhead college savings program participants gain new ESG investment menu options; defined benefit plan members and non-self-directed portfolios are unaffected.
deep_poi: This is a DC-menu-design and disclosure bill, not a benefit-design bill: it touches no multiplier, COLA, contribution rate, or funding policy, so its fiscal footprint is administrative (WSIB staff/reporting time and investment product development), not actuarial, despite the bill's pension classification.

The mandate reaches only self-directed plan 3 accounts (TRS/SERS/PERS 3), ABLE, and DreamAhead participants, not the far larger commingled DB trust funds where WSIB already reports it 'broadly incorporates' ESG considerations per the intent section, so the operative options requirement is a narrow slice of total WSIB-managed assets.

Section 3 reenacts and amends RCW 43.33A.190 citing two separate 2016 amendments to the same section (2016 c 69 s 20 and 2016 c 39 s 8), a code-reviser reconciliation of parallel 2016 changes rather than a substantive policy signal, but it adds drafting complexity worth checking against the current RCW text.

No emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause, and no contingent effective date despite a hard January 1, 2024 implementation deadline for both the report and the new investment options, so funding and timing risk for meeting that deadline is not addressed in the bill text itself.
deep_oneLine: HB 1283 requires the Washington State Investment Board to publicly report every three years on climate-related financial risk and governance practices across its portfolios, and to offer at least three ESG-aligned investment options to plan 3 and self-directed program participants by January 1, 2024.

brief: Concerning cost-of-living adjustments for plan 1 retirees of the teachers' retirement system and public employees' retirement system.
haiku_summary: Establishes indexed cost-of-living adjustments for Plan 1 retirees in the Teachers' Retirement System and Public Employees' Retirement System, capped at three percent annually.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 41.32 RCW directing the department, beginning July 1, 2023 and annually thereafter, to compute a ratio-based COLA for each TRS Plan 1 retired member or beneficiary whose allowance has been in effect at least one year, using the ratio of CPI-W (Seattle area) for the year before determination to CPI-W for the year before July 1, 2022 (or the retirement date if later), applied against the original allowance as of June 30, 2023.
Identical new section added to chapter 41.40 RCW establishing the same ratio-based, CPI-W-indexed COLA mechanism for PERS Plan 1 retired members and beneficiaries.
Limits the new COLA to plan 1 retired members or beneficiaries whose retirement allowance has been in effect for at least one year at the time of determination.

Caps the adjustment so it can never reduce the allowance below the original amount, can never exceed 3 percent in the first annual adjustment, and cannot change from the prior year's adjustment by more than 3 percentage points.
Section 3 declares the act necessary for the immediate preservation of public peace, health, or safety and sets a fixed effective date of July 1, 2023, with no appropriation contingency attached.

deep_whoAffected: TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 retirees and beneficiaries with at least one year on the retirement rolls; Plan 2/3 members and other retirement systems (LEOFF, WSPRS, SERS, etc.) are not touched.
deep_poi: The formula duplicates the existing 'Uniform COLA' design already used elsewhere in the plan 2/3 systems (index-ratio to a base year, floor at original allowance, 3 percent annual cap), effectively extending that mechanism to the plan 1 cohort rather than inventing new COLA math.

No funding or appropriation provision accompanies the benefit increase; the bill carries an emergency clause and a fixed July 1, 2023 effective date rather than a contingent-on-appropriation clause, so enactment is not conditioned on the budget providing the money.

Because the year-over-year change is capped at 3 percentage points but the underlying ratio is measured against a fixed original-allowance base rather than compounding off the prior year's adjusted amount, a high-inflation stretch (2022 CPI was elevated) could produce a ratio above 3 percent that gets truncated in year one, with permanent under-indexing baked in if CPI outpaces the 3-point year-over-year cap in subsequent years.

Sections 1 and 2 are verbatim duplicates targeted at different chapters (41.32 for TRS, 41.40 for PERS), which is standard drafting practice for parallel plan 1 provisions but means any future amendment must be made in both places to stay in sync.
deep_oneLine: HB 1294 creates an annual CPI-indexed cost-of-living adjustment for TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 retirees, capped at 3 percent per year, with an emergency clause taking effect July 1, 2023.

brief: Adding references to contractor registration and licensing laws in workers' compensation, public works, and prevailing wage statutes.
triage_how: The bill adds contractor registration and licensing references to workers' compensation and public works statutes without affecting public retirement benefits or systems.

brief: Splitting the volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund into two accounts.
triage_how: The bill splits a Washington public pension system (volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension system) into two separate plans to maintain IRS qualification status.

brief: Concerning property exempt from execution.
triage_how: The bill protects workers' compensation and general personal property from garnishment and execution but does not affect public employee retirement systems or benefits.

brief: Concerning flexible work for general and limited authority Washington peace officers.
haiku_summary: The bill expands membership eligibility in the Law Enforcement Officers' and Firefighters' Retirement System by allowing part-time, fully compensated law enforcement officers to qualify as law enforcement officers for pension purposes.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds new RCW 41.26.030(19)(f): beginning July 1, 2023, "law enforcement officer" also includes a person commissioned and employed on a fully compensated but less-than-full-time basis, so long as they meet the other qualifications in (a)-(e) of the subsection.
Conforming amendment to RCW 41.26.030(19)(c) states the full-time requirement for commissioned city police personnel does not apply to the extent allowed under new (19)(f).

Strikes "full-time," from the RCW 10.93.020 definitions of "general authority Washington peace officer" (4) and "limited authority Washington peace officer" (6), so part-time fully compensated officers qualify as peace officers for mutual-aid/commissioning purposes under chapter 10.93 RCW, not just for LEOFF.

Adds a new uncodified section to chapter 49.28 RCW authorizing (but not requiring) law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies, barring layoff or displacement of full-time officers, preserving existing collective bargaining agreements and the duty to bargain, and requiring full-time and part-time officers at the same agency to be in the same bargaining unit.

Newly LEOFF-eligible part-time officers will accrue service credit under the existing Plan 2 hours-based partial-month schedule (full credit at 90+ hours/month, half credit at 70-89 hours, quarter credit below 70 hours); the bill does not create a new accrual rule for this group.

Updates an internal cross-reference in the emergency medical technician clause of the "firefighter" definition from RCW 18.73.030(12) to 18.73.030(13), a non-substantive recodification fix unrelated to the flexible-work policy.

deep_whoAffected: General authority and limited authority Washington peace officers who are fully compensated but work part time (and the LEOFF employers that choose to use them); full-time officers, firefighters, and Plan 1 members are not directly affected by the definitional change.
deep_poi: The membership expansion runs entirely through a definitional gateway (deleting "full-time" from RCW 41.26.030(19) and RCW 10.93.020) rather than a standalone eligibility or funding section, so its actuarial footprint depends on how many agencies actually adopt part-time policies under the new chapter 49.28 RCW authority - nothing in the bill text itself quantifies or caps that exposure.

No benefit formula, multiplier, vesting, or contribution-rate provision is touched; any cost effect is carried entirely through the existing Plan 2 hours-based partial service-credit schedule (quarter/half/full month), which was written for other purposes (e.g., mid-month hires, reduced schedules) and is now the mechanism by which a new class of intentionally part-time officers earns pension service.

"Beginning July 1, 2023" is embedded directly in the substantive definition (RCW 41.26.030(19)(f)) rather than set by a conventional bill effective-date section - an unusual drafting choice that, given this substitute's February 2023 first reading, could predate the bill's actual enactment and effective date, creating a quasi-retroactive application window for eligibility.

Section 1 is enabling only (agencies "may" adopt a flexible work policy) and explicitly forecloses a two-tier bargaining structure - full-time and part-time officers at the same employer must remain in the same bargaining unit - which limits the cost-shifting or labor-cost-arbitrage risk that a part-time carve-out might otherwise invite.
deep_oneLine: SHB 1413 lets Washington law enforcement agencies adopt voluntary flexible/part-time work policies for peace officers and, by striking "full-time" from the officer definitions in RCW 41.26.030 (LEOFF) and RCW 10.93.020, opens LEOFF Plan 2 membership and peace-officer status to fully compensated officers who work less than full time, effective July 1, 2023.

brief: Providing an annual adjustment in the public employees' retirement system and teachers' retirement system plan 1 benefits capped at $110 per month by adjusting the long-term investment rate of return assumption.
haiku_summary: The bill establishes an annual cost-of-living adjustment for PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retired beneficiaries, capped at $110 per month increase, and lowers the long-term investment return assumption to 7.2 percent.

deep_provisions.detail: Creates a new annual postretirement adjustment for TRS Plan 1 retirees/beneficiaries retired at least one year, based on the ratio of the current year's Seattle-area CPI to the CPI at retirement (or July 2022 base), applied each July.
deep_provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.32 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: Creates an identical new annual postretirement adjustment for PERS Plan 1 retirees/beneficiaries retired at least one year, using the same CPI-ratio methodology and same July effective date.
deep_provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.40 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: Caps the adjustment so it can never reduce the original allowance, cannot exceed 3 percent in the first year, cannot change by more than 3 percentage points from the prior year's adjustment, and cannot raise the monthly benefit by more than $110 over the prior year's amount.
deep_provisions.cites: new sections to chapters 41.32 and 41.40 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: States the legislature reserves the right to amend or repeal the new COLA provision at any time and that no member or beneficiary has a contractual right to an adjustment not already granted.
deep_provisions.cites: new sections to chapters 41.32 and 41.40 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: Amends the long-term investment rate of return assumption used by the state actuary, adding a new tier that lowers it from 7.7 percent (set in 2017) to 7.2 percent beginning July 1, 2023, a smaller reduction than the Pension Funding Council's 2021 recommendation of 7.0 percent.

Section 1 legislative findings declare the benefit increase and the investment rate of return change to be an integrated, nonseverable package, even though Section 5 contains a standard severability clause stating that if any provision is held invalid the remainder of the act stays in effect.

deep_whoAffected: PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retirees and beneficiaries who have been retired at least one year gain a capped CPI-linked COLA; PERS/TRS Plan 2 and 3 members and other retirement systems are unaffected, and all system members are affected indirectly through the changed investment return assumption used to value their plans.
deep_poi: Section 1's uncodified findings assert the act's provisions are 'nonseverable,' but the operative Section 5 is a conventional severability clause preserving the rest of the act if any part is struck down — a direct textual conflict likely to draw scrutiny in any legal challenge.

The bill lowers the assumed investment rate of return only to 7.2 percent rather than the Pension Funding Council's recommended 7.0 percent, effectively pairing a smaller actuarial conservatism increase with the new COLA cost, a deliberate tradeoff flagged in the findings themselves.

The COLA is narrowly targeted: only Plan 1 members retired at least one year as of the July determination date qualify, and the $110/month and 3 percent caps mean the adjustment will lag actual CPI growth in high-inflation years, especially for higher-dollar allowances.

The 'no contractual right' / legislative reservation clause in both new sections signals this is designed as a discretionary, revocable benefit rather than a vested one, consistent with past legislative caution after Plan 1 COLA litigation history.
deep_oneLine: HB 1459 grants PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retirees a capped cost-of-living adjustment (3% per year, $110/month maximum increase) tied to the Seattle-area CPI, funded in part by only partially lowering the assumed long-term investment rate of return (from 7.7% to 7.2%, RCW 41.45.035), with an emergency clause and a legislative declaration that the act's provisions are nonseverable.

No pension provisos, contribution rate suspensions, benefit changes, or fiscal maneuvers touching retirement funds are present in this bill.

The single hit outside RCW 43.84.092 (line 476) concerns public-disclosure exemptions for city retirement board investment records, an incidental carryover from amending an adjacent public-records subsection, not a pension policy change.

brief: Permitting general authority peace officers certificated by the criminal justice training commission and employed on a full-time basis by the government of a federally recognized tribe to participate in the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system plan 2.
haiku_summary: The bill extends membership in the Law Enforcement Officers' and Firefighters' Retirement System Plan 2 to certified peace officers employed full-time by federally recognized tribes, subject to state-tribal compacts that require employer contributions and establish participation requirements.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds the government of a federally recognized tribe to the definition of a general authority law enforcement agency.

Adds a new subsection defining law enforcement officer to include a person employed on or after January 1, 2024 by a tribal police department under a section 2 compact who is certified as a general authority peace officer under chapter 43.101 RCW.
Renumbers a cross reference to RCW 18.73.030 from subsection (12) to (13), a conforming technical fix flagged by the reviser's note, not a substantive change.

Authorizes the governor to negotiate and execute state-tribal compacts admitting tribal general authority peace officers into LEOFF Plan 2, with an application process, a 90-day government-to-government meeting requirement, and mandatory compact terms covering employer status, reporting/contribution/auditing compliance, a limited waiver of sovereign immunity and consent to state court jurisdiction, dissolution and withdrawal-liability procedures, and acknowledgment of possible federal tax consequences.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 2)

deep_provisions.detail: Provides that the pension-participation portions of a compact are null and void if the IRS finds them in conflict with governmental plan qualification requirements under IRC section 401(a) and the conflict cannot be resolved administratively or by amendment.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 2(6)(g))

deep_provisions.detail: Provides that tribal law enforcement employees of a tribe that opts out of pension participation earn no service credit in the plan.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 2(7))

deep_provisions.detail: Requires tribal governments participating through a state-tribal compact to contribute both the employer and state shares of retirement system cost for their LEOFF officers, the same funding obligation currently imposed on port districts and higher-education institutions.

Allows a tribal officer employed by a tribal police department on July 1, 2025 to purchase service credit for qualifying prior service, with a written election due by June 30, 2026 and full actuarial-cost payment required within five years of the election or before retirement, whichever comes first.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 4)

deep_provisions.detail: Sets the act's effective date as July 1, 2025.

deep_whoAffected: Certificated general authority peace officers employed full-time by tribal police departments of federally recognized tribes in Washington that opt into a state-tribal compact; a narrow new LEOFF Plan 2 membership class, with existing LEOFF 2 members and non-tribal employers otherwise unaffected.
deep_poi: Creates a novel compact-based admission mechanism for a sovereign tribal government into a state pension system, including a negotiated limited waiver of tribal sovereign immunity and consent to state court jurisdiction for enforcement purposes, a precedent-setting design not used elsewhere in LEOFF.

Shifts the full funding burden onto participating tribes: RCW 41.26.450 makes tribal employers pay both the employer and the state contribution shares, unlike the normal three-way employee/employer/state split, so the state bears no ongoing normal-cost share for this new class.

Anticipates instability with explicit withdrawal-liability and dissolution procedures plus a null-and-void clause tied to future IRS guidance on IRC 401(a) governmental plan qualification, reflecting unresolved federal tax-law uncertainty about tribal government participation in a state retirement system.

Section 4's prior-service purchase window (elect by June 30, 2026, pay full actuarial cost) is self-funded by the member rather than subsidized, limiting cost/gaming risk to the plan, but the narrow eligibility date (must be employed on July 1, 2025) and short election window create a hard cutoff for who can buy in.
deep_oneLine: HB 1481 lets Washington tribal governments elect, through a negotiated state-tribal compact, to enroll certificated general authority peace officers employed by tribal police departments in LEOFF Plan 2, with participating tribes paying both the employer and state contribution shares and a limited window to purchase prior service credit.

hidden_passages.where: Line 36, definitions section, "(19) 'Disposable earnings'"
hidden_passages.what: Defines disposable earnings for purposes of garnishing/withholding legal financial obligations (LFOs) from offenders. States that 'disposable earnings' specifically includes periodic payments pursuant to pension or retirement programs, or insurance policies of any type (with carve-outs for Title 50 and Title 74 RCW payments). This is standard definitional boilerplate carried over from existing RCW 9.94A.030 language, not new policy — it just clarifies that a convicted person's pension/retirement income counts as garnishable earnings when the court is collecting LFOs.

hidden_poi: The bill's true term count for genuine pension vocabulary (word-boundary match on 'pension', 'retirement', 'actuari', 'LEOFF', 'deferred compensation', 'department of retirement') is 1, not 31.

The classifier's 31-count almost certainly comes from naive substring matching: 'pension' appears inside 'suspension' 18 times (this is a DUI/license-suspension bill, so 'suspension' is everywhere), and 'PERS' (a WA pension-system acronym) appears inside common words like 'offenders', 'supersede', 'dispersed', etc. 108 times.

No amendments to Title 41 RCW (public pension systems), no LEOFF/PERS/TRS/SERS/PSERS/WSPRS statutory references, no actuarial or contribution-rate language, no appropriations provisos touching retirement funds anywhere in the bill text.

Conclusion for the pension-classification project: this is a clean example of a false positive that should be excluded from any 'hidden pension policy' list — recommend tightening the term-matching regex to use word boundaries before rerunning the classifier corpus-wide, since other bills flagged the same way (e.g., other traffic/suspension-heavy bills) likely have the same artifact.

brief: Creating a separate fund for the purposes of self-insured pensions and assessments.
triage_how: Creates a separate state treasury fund to hold reserves from self-insured workers' compensation employers without affecting public retirement systems or benefits.

brief: Concerning vacation leave accrual for state employees.
haiku_summary: The bill increases state employee vacation leave accrual limits from 240 to 280 hours while explicitly excluding such excess leave from retirement benefit calculations to prevent pension inflation.

deep_provisions.detail: Raises the maximum accrued unused vacation leave a state officer/employee may carry from 240 to 280 hours (both the base cap and the extended cap available under a retained statement-of-necessity).

Conforms the alternative no-statement-of-necessity accumulation method's trigger threshold from 'in excess of 240 hours' to 'in excess of 280 hours,' matching the new base accrual cap in RCW 43.01.040.
Non-substantive drafting correction changing 'as [at] a minimum' to 'at a minimum' in the statement-of-necessity content requirements.

Adds an express cap limiting vacation-leave payout upon termination of employment to 'up to 240 hours,' even though the underlying accrual cap in RCW 43.01.040 is being raised to 280 hours, so up to 40 accrued hours become non-cashable at separation under this section.

Removes the cross-reference to RCW 43.01.044 and 43.01.041 from the PERS 'compensation earnable' exclusion for unused annual leave in excess of 240 hours, decoupling that pension-compensation exclusion threshold from the general leave statutes so a future change to the accrual/payout caps does not automatically alter what counts as pensionable compensation.

Converts numerous spelled-out numbers to numerals throughout the PERS definitions section (e.g., fifty-nine to 59, sixty to 60, twelve to 12, ten to 10, seventy to 70, twenty-two to 22, forty-five to 45, thirty-three to 33, eleven to 11) as non-substantive code-revision style cleanup with no benefit change.

Adds a new exclusion to the WSPRS 'salary' definition for members commissioned prior to July 1, 2001, excluding lump-sum payments for unused accumulated vacation or annual leave in excess of 240 hours (plus hours earned since the member's anniversary date) from countable salary, bringing that cohort into parity with the exclusion language already applicable to members commissioned on or after July 1, 2001.

deep_whoAffected: All state officers and employees for general vacation-accrual purposes; PERS Plan 1/2/3 members and WSPRS Plan 1/2 members for the pension-compensation and cash-out provisions, with a narrow carve-out benefiting WSPRS members commissioned before July 1, 2001
deep_poi: The bill raises the working accrual cap (240 to 280 hours) but deliberately holds the PERS compensation-earnable exclusion and the RCW 43.01.041 termination cash-out cap at 240 hours, an apparent anti-spiking design that expands a leave benefit without expanding pensionable compensation.

Severing the cross-reference in RCW 41.40.010(8)(a)(ii)(B) to RCW 43.01.044 and 43.01.041 is a notable drafting choice: it insulates the PERS compensation-earnable definition from future amendments to the general leave-accrual statutes, a precedent worth flagging for anyone tracking how pension definitions get decoupled from HR policy statutes.

The new WSPRS carve-out for members commissioned before July 1, 2001 is narrow and technical, but its existence implies that, absent this fix, that specific legacy cohort's salary definition may not have excluded large unused-leave cash-outs the way later cohorts' definitions already do, a potential prior spiking exposure for a small closed group.

The bulk of the RCW 41.40.010 changes are cosmetic numeral-for-spelled-number conversions, which could make the one substantive change in that section (the cross-reference removal in (8)(a)(ii)(B)) easy to overlook on a quick read.
deep_oneLine: HB 1566 raises the general state-employee vacation-leave accrual cap from 240 to 280 hours (RCW 43.01.040/.044) but freezes the PERS compensation-earnable exclusion and the termination cash-out cap at 240 hours, so the added leave does not flow into pensionable compensation, while adding a narrow WSPRS salary-exclusion fix for troopers commissioned before July 1, 2001.

triage_how: The bill concerns health insurance benefits through the Public Employees Benefits Board for retirees, not Washington public retirement income systems or pension plans.

brief: Concerning the reemployment and pension service credit of public employees separated from service due to a vaccination mandate.
haiku_summary: The bill allows public employees separated from service due to employer vaccination mandates to receive up to five years of retirement system service credit upon return to covered employment if they make required contributions.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds a new subsection to RCW 41.26.520 (LEOFF 2) granting up to five years of retirement service credit for members who left employment, voluntarily or involuntarily, due to an employer vaccination mandate imposed after January 1, 2020.
Adds an identical vaccination-mandate service-credit purchase provision to RCW 41.32.810 (TRS 2/3 leave-of-absence/military service statute).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.32.865 (TRS defined-benefit/defined-contribution hybrid plan leave provisions).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.35.470 (SERS 2/3).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.35.650 (SERS Plan 3/hybrid leave provisions).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.37.260 (PSERS).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.40.710 (PERS 2).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 41.40.805 (PERS Plan 3 hybrid leave provisions).
Adds the same vaccination-mandate service-credit provision to RCW 43.43.260 (WSPRS 2) and folds the new subsection into the existing 75 percent of average-final-salary benefit cap.

To claim the credit, a returning member must apply within 90 days of resuming covered employment and pay employee contributions (plus interest) within five years of resumption or before retirement, or, if those deadlines are missed, pay the alternative amount under RCW 41.50.165(2) prior to retirement.

Once the member pays the employee share, the administering department bills the former employer for its share of the plan-appropriate contributions (RCW 41.45.060, 41.45.061, and 41.45.067, or equivalent chapter cites) plus interest, for the separation period, shifting the employer contribution liability retroactively to employers who imposed the mandate.

Compensation used to calculate required contributions is the pay the member would have earned absent the mandate-related separation, or, if that cannot be reasonably estimated, the compensation reported for the member in the year before the separation (mirrors the existing military-leave compensation-estimation method).

New freestanding section adds a hiring preference in all state and local government (and contracted private) competitive civil-service examinations for applicants separated from any employment due to vaccination status in 2020-2022, adding 10 percent to the applicant's passing score.

Preference is self-certified: the applicant submits either proof of dismissal for vaccination status or proof of the prior employer's vaccination policy plus an affidavit of separation due to that policy; no independent verification mechanism is specified.

Legislative findings section recounts Executive Order 22-13's state workforce losses (about 1,900 employees including 400 transportation workers) and the state's subsequent shift from a vaccine-booster mandate to a $1,000 incentive payment, framing the bill's intent to facilitate rehiring and restore service credit.

deep_whoAffected: Members of LEOFF Plan 2, TRS Plans 2/3, SERS Plans 2/3, PSERS, PERS Plans 2/3, and WSPRS Plan 2 who separated from public employment (voluntarily or involuntarily) due to an employer COVID-19 vaccination mandate imposed after January 1, 2020, and who later return to covered employment; also job applicants statewide who were dismissed for vaccination status.
deep_poi: The employer contribution liability for the missed-service period is billed to the employer that imposed the mandate rather than shared prospectively across the plan, so the fiscal exposure lands narrowly on state agencies and local governments that had vaccination policies -- a targeted retroactive cost-shift rather than a systemwide funding change.

The bill defines the eligible population by a specific historical cause of separation (employer vaccination mandate after January 1, 2020) rather than by an ongoing plan feature, which is an unusual, one-time cohort carve-out layered into the general military-leave service-credit framework across nine separate RCW sections -- meaning any actuarial cost estimate depends entirely on how many separated employees actually return and buy back credit, a population that is hard to size ex ante.

The hiring-preference mechanism in the new chapter 41.04 section relies on applicant self-certification (affidavit plus policy proof) with no stated verification standard, which invites disputes over eligibility and potential inconsistency in how examining bodies apply the 10-point boost.

Six of nine amended sections are the DC/hybrid-plan leave-of-absence provisions (TRS/SERS/PERS Plan 3 and PSERS/WSPRS structures) where the mechanics of billing 'employer contributions' plus interest into a defined contribution account for a multi-year retroactive gap could pose administrative complications not present in straight defined-benefit plans.

The bill carries both an emergency clause and immediate effective date, atypical for a service-credit purchase bill of this kind, suggesting the sponsors intended fast implementation ahead of further changes to state vaccination policy referenced in the intent section.
deep_oneLine: HB 1814 creates a new vaccination-mandate service-credit purchase right (up to five years) in LEOFF 2, TRS 2/3, SERS 2/3, PSERS, PERS 2/3, and WSPRS, adds a 10-point hiring-exam preference for employees separated over vaccination status, and takes effect immediately as an emergency measure.
