Embedded in that list, unchanged, are: the deferred compensation administrative account, the deferred compensation principal account, the department of retirement systems expense account, the judges' retirement account, the judicial retirement administrative account, the judicial retirement principal account, the pension funding stabilization account, the public employees' retirement system plan 1 account, the public employees' retirement system combined plan 2 and plan 3 account, the higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund, the money-purchase retirement savings administrative and principal accounts, the supplemental pension account, the teachers' retirement system plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, the volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, the Washington judicial retirement system account, the LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, the Washington public safety employees' plan 2 retirement account, and the Washington school employees' retirement system combined plan 2 and 3 account, plus several 'retirement fund' bond-redemption accounts (ferry, highway, University of Washington, WSU, transportation improvement board) that are debt-service funds unrelated to pensions.

hidden_passages.where: Same two lines, the only marked edit within either paragraph
hidden_passages.what: An <TextRun amendingStyle="add">JUDY</TextRun> tag inserts the word 'JUDY' before 'transportation future funding program account,' renaming that single (non-pension) transportation account. No other word in either paragraph carries an amendingStyle tag — the entire retirement/pension portion of the list is reproduced verbatim as surrounding statutory context, not amended.

hidden_poi: All 24 pension-term hits trace to just two lines of the bill (136, 282), which are duplicate copies of the same section (likely one original enactment and one recodification/reenactment pass typical of transportation revenue acts).

Both instances are the standard RCW 43.79A.040 'distribution of income' laundry list that appears in nearly every biennial transportation budget or transportation-account bill; it lists every state account/fund, pension and non-pension alike, that shares in treasury interest earnings by average daily balance.
No pension RCW chapter (41.xx) is opened, cited as amended, or cross-referenced substantively anywhere in the bill body outside this list.
No contribution rate, benefit formula, actuarial valuation, funding method, or DRS administrative authority language appears anywhere in the file.

The bill's only substantive edit intersecting this paragraph is the 'JUDY' renaming of a transportation (non-retirement) account, confirming the pension account names are incidental carryover text, not the target of the amendment.
This is a clean negative case for the classifier question: high raw term-count from a boilerplate omnibus account list, zero substantive pension policy content.

brief: Reducing the number of days that a worker's temporary total disability must continue to receive industrial insurance compensation for the day of an injury and the three-day period following the injury.
triage_how: The bill modifies workers' compensation temporary total disability eligibility without affecting public retirement systems or benefits.

brief: Including in the public safety employees' retirement system specified competency restoration workers at department of social and health services institutional and residential sites that serve civilly committed residents or serve patients under not guilty by reason of insanity findings.
haiku_summary: The bill expands Public Safety Employees' Retirement System membership eligibility to include competency restoration workers at Department of Social and Health Services institutional sites serving civilly committed residents or patients under not guilty by reason of insanity findings.

deep_provisions.detail: Amends the PSERS Plan 2 definition of "member" to add workers at DSHS/DCYF institutions or residential sites that serve civilly committed residents or patients found not guilty by reason of insanity, alongside the existing competency-restoration and developmentally-disabled categories (state-operated living alternatives facilities remain excluded).

Gives an employee who was in PERS Plan 2 or 3 immediately before the effective date and who meets the newly expanded eligibility criteria a one-time choice, during an election period running from the effective date to September 1, 2025, to stay in PERS or become a PSERS Plan 2 dual member under chapter 41.54 RCW.
deep_provisions.cites: New section, chapter 41.37 RCW; chapter 41.54 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: Bars transfer of service credit accrued in PERS into PSERS for employees who elect to switch; the PSERS membership is prospective only from the date of election.
Employees not electing by September 1, 2025 default to staying in their current PERS plan permanently, with no automatic PSERS conversion.
Employees who were PERS Plan 1 members on or before June 1, 2019 and later work in a newly eligible position remain in PERS Plan 1; they are not offered the PSERS election.
All new hires on or after the effective date who fill a newly eligible position become PSERS Plan 2 members automatically, with no election.
Sets the act's effective date at June 1, 2025, a year after the June 1, 2024 effective date of the underlying 2023 c 199 definitional section being amended.

deep_whoAffected: DSHS/DCYF institutional and residential-site workers who provide custody, nursing, or security services to civilly committed residents or NGRI patients (competency restoration-adjacent staff), currently covered by PERS Plan 1, 2, or 3, gain PSERS Plan 2 eligibility; PERS Plan 1 members in that population are excluded from the new option and stay put.
deep_poi: The mechanism is dual membership under ch. 41.54 RCW with no PERS-to-PSERS service credit transfer, so the bill avoids shifting accrued PERS liability onto PSERS; the actuarial cost is limited to prospective service and any dual-membership benefit calculation effects, not a stock of transferred credit.

PERS Plan 1 members are affirmatively locked out of the election and must remain in Plan 1, consistent with the closed, legislatively protected status of Plan 1 and avoidance of moving Plan 1's distinct funding and benefit structure into PSERS.

A roughly 15-month, one-time election window (effective date to September 1, 2025) is a self-selection design: analysts would expect adverse selection toward PSERS by employees for whom the more generous PSERS 2%/60 formula and earlier retirement age outweigh PERS terms, which OSA would need to model as a participation-rate assumption rather than a known cost.

Eligibility turns on fact-specific site/duty classifications ("serve civilly committed residents," "serve patients under not guilty by reason of insanity findings") layered onto existing competency-restoration language; boundary calls about which specific institutions or rotating staff qualify could generate classification disputes similar to those seen in other PSERS carve-outs.
deep_oneLine: HB 1949 expands the PSERS Plan 2 "member" definition (RCW 41.37.010(19)(d)(iv)) to cover DSHS institutional/residential competency restoration workers who serve civilly committed residents or NGRI patients, and creates a new section letting current PERS Plan 2/3 employees at those sites elect, through September 1, 2025, to become PSERS Plan 2 dual members without transferring PERS service credit, while PERS Plan 1 members at those sites remain in Plan 1 and new hires are placed directly into PSERS.

brief: Providing a benefit increase to certain retirees of the public employees' retirement system plan 1 and the teachers' retirement system plan 1.
haiku_summary: The bill provides a one-time cost-of-living adjustment of 3 percent (capped at $110 per month) effective July 1, 2024, to beneficiaries of the Teachers' Retirement System Plan 1 and Public Employees' Retirement System Plan 1 who were receiving monthly benefits on July 1, 2023.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (5) to RCW 41.32.4992 granting TRS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2023 a 3 percent increase to that benefit, capped at $110.00, effective July 1, 2024.

Adds new subsection (5) to RCW 41.40.1987 granting PERS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2023 a 3 percent increase to that benefit, capped at $110.00, effective July 1, 2024.
Renumbers the exclusion clause as subsection (6) and retains that the TRS increase does not apply to those receiving benefits under RCW 41.32.489 or 41.32.540.
Renumbers the exclusion clause as subsection (6) and retains that the PERS increase does not apply to those receiving benefits under RCW 41.40.1984.

deep_whoAffected: Retirees and beneficiaries of TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 who were on the benefit rolls as of July 1, 2023, excluding those already receiving benefits under the separate minimum-benefit provisions of RCW 41.32.489, 41.32.540, and 41.40.1984.
deep_poi: This is the fifth consecutive one-time, non-compounding ad hoc increase layered onto closed Plan 1 systems (2018, 2020, 2022, 2023, now 2024), each keyed to a snapshot date of who is on the rolls, rather than an ongoing COLA; the dollar cap has been frozen at $110 for three cycles running, so the cap itself has not kept pace with inflation.

The bill continues the pattern set by 2023 c 397, whose uncodified finding stated an ongoing COLA "may not be affordable until required employer contribution rates towards the unfunded accrued actuarial liability are reduced or no longer required" and directed SCPP to study a permanent COLA during the 2023-25 biennium; this bill enacts another one-time patch rather than the studied permanent fix, leaving that study mandate unresolved.

No emergency clause and no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause appear in this bill's own text, unlike its 2023 c 397 predecessor which carried an immediate-effective-date emergency clause; worth confirming the bill's effective date against its internal July 1, 2024 trigger date.

Eligibility is a point-in-time snapshot (on the rolls as of July 1, 2023) rather than continuous eligibility through the effective date, which is standard for this series but worth checking against survivor benefit rules for any edge-case windfalls if status changes between snapshot and effective date.
deep_oneLine: SHB 1985 extends the annual one-time ad hoc benefit increase for TRS Plan 1 and PERS Plan 1 retirees by adding a fifth increment: beneficiaries on the rolls as of July 1, 2023 get a 3 percent increase, capped at $110/month, effective July 1, 2024.

brief: Paying state retirement benefits until the end of the month in which the retiree or beneficiary dies.
haiku_summary: The state will continue paying retirement benefits through the end of the month in which a retiree or beneficiary dies, instead of requiring repayment of benefits received after the precise date of death.

deep_provisions.detail: Requires DRS to continue paying retiree or beneficiary benefits through the end of the month in which death occurs, rather than stopping precisely on the date of death, across all listed retirement systems.
deep_provisions.cites: New section, chapter 41.50 RCW; applies to retirees/beneficiaries under chapters 2.10, 2.12, 41.26, 41.32, 41.35, 41.37, 41.40, and 43.43 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: Sets the start date for survivor benefits at the first day of the month following the month in which the retiree or beneficiary died, coordinating with the new month-end payment rule.
Clarifies that the month-end payment rule applies to all benefit payments issued by DRS, including optional annuities, not just standard periodic retirement allowances.

Preserves DRS's existing authority and obligation to require the beneficiary, survivor, or estate to refund any benefit payments issued for periods after the month of death, so the fix shifts the recovery cutoff to month-end but does not eliminate overpayment recovery.
Makes the new rule prospective only, expressly stating that no beneficiary, survivor, or estate that repaid benefits before January 1, 2025 has any right to a refund of those prior repayments.

deep_whoAffected: Retirees, beneficiaries, survivors, and estates across essentially all state retirement systems (PERS, TRS, SERS/PSERS, LEOFF, WSPRS, and judicial retirement under chapters 2.10, 2.12, 41.26, 41.32, 41.35, 41.37, 41.40, and 43.43 RCW) whose death occurs mid-month; estates of decedents dying mid-month gain a partial month of retained benefits, while estates of those who already repaid pre-2025 overpayments gain nothing.
deep_poi: A single new section in chapter 41.50 RCW (the general DRS administration chapter) reaches into eight separate retirement-system chapters at once, rather than amending each system's statute individually, a centralization approach rather than parallel system-by-system amendments.

Subsection (4) affirmatively forecloses refund claims from estates that already repaid pre-2025 overpayments under the old date-of-death cutoff, a defensive drafting choice that limits the state's retroactive liability exposure rather than extending equitable relief to past cases.

The bill does not eliminate DRS's overpayment recovery power; subsection (3) keeps clawback authority intact for payments beyond the new month-end cutoff, so the change is narrowly a shift in the cutoff date, not a broader forgiveness of overpayments.

By request of the Select Committee on Pension Policy (SCPP), signaling this originated as a technical administrative-correction bill rather than a benefit-expansion policy initiative, consistent with its narrow, mechanical scope.
deep_oneLine: HB 2013 adds a new section to chapter 41.50 RCW directing DRS to continue paying retiree and beneficiary benefits through the end of the month in which death occurs (rather than stopping on the exact death date), delays survivor benefits to the first of the following month, preserves DRS's authority to recover payments issued after month-end, and bars retroactive refund claims for repayments already made before the January 1, 2025 effective date.

brief: Concerning the definition of veteran and restoring honor to veterans.
haiku_summary: The bill expands the definition of veteran to include those with non-honorable discharges who have VA benefits or were discharged due to sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression, making them eligible for military service credit in public pension calculations.

deep_provisions.detail: Creates a new statutory "qualifying discharge" definition (new section, ch. 73.04 RCW) that includes honorable, general-under-honorable, other-than-honorable-with-VA-monetary-benefits, and any discharge motivated solely by sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression (or related statements/conduct/disclosure), and applies it across roughly 19 cross-referenced RCW sections governing licensing, tuition, hunting/fishing, gambling-license renewal, and civil-service employment preference.

Strikes the cross-reference to RCW 41.16.220, 41.20.050, and 41.40.170 from the RCW 41.04.005 "veteran" definition being broadened, and instead rewrites those three sections to spell out "honorably discharged" (or honorable-record physical discharge) with period-of-war service directly, so PERS and old-law police/fire pension military service-credit purchase does not inherit the act's broadened qualifying-discharge standard.

Reenacts and amends RCW 41.40.170 (PERS military service credit purchase) to require the member be "an honorably discharged veteran or veteran who received a physical discharge from the armed forces with an honorable record" and to affirmatively prove period-of-war service under RCW 41.04.005, tightening the drafting even as it fixes an internal citation error (41.40.005 to 41.04.005).

Reenacts and amends RCW 41.20.050 (old-law city police pension) to require honorable discharge (or honorable-record physical discharge) during a period of war for military-service credit toward the 25-year pension calculation.

Amends RCW 84.39.020 to allow the deceased-veteran property tax exemption for surviving spouses even where the veteran had an other-than-honorable discharge, provided the veteran or survivor was eligible for or received federal VA monetary benefits.

Amends RCW 28B.15.012 to apply the qualifying-discharge standard to resident-tuition eligibility for veterans and their dependents, while retaining exclusion of students with bad-conduct discharge, officer dismissal, or dishonorable discharge.

Repeals RCW 2.48.100 (bar admission, effect of disability discharge) and RCW 73.04.042 (1919/1923 honorable-discharge recording statute for Spanish-American War and WWI veterans) as obsolete honorable-discharge-based provisions superseded by the qualifying-discharge standard.
Adds a new section directing the Department of Veterans Affairs to develop and implement an outreach program informing veterans of the law's changes, beginning on that section's effective date.

deep_whoAffected: Veterans/former service members with general-under-honorable, other-than-honorable (VA-benefit-eligible), or LGBTQ+ bias-motivated discharges gain expanded state licensing, tuition, hunting/fishing, employment-preference, and veterans'-home benefits; the same members are excluded from gaining expanded PERS/old-law police and fire pension military service credit, which retains the narrower honorable-discharge/period-of-war standard.
deep_poi: The bill's headline reform (a broadened "qualifying discharge" standard reaching LGBTQ+ bias discharges and other-than-honorable-with-VA-benefits cases) is deliberately not extended to RCW 41.40.170 (PERS military service credit) or RCW 41.20.050/41.16.220 (predecessor police/fire pension military credit) — Sec. 2 strips those three RCW cites from the definition's scope and Secs. 18-20 restate "honorably discharged"/period-of-war language directly, so bad-paper veterans gain tuition, licensing, and hunting benefits but not retirement service credit purchase eligibility.

Section 40 makes the entire act null and void without a specific appropriation identified by bill or chapter number in the omnibus budget by June 30, 2024 — a funding contingency that would also nullify the pension-carve-out drafting itself if unfunded.

Section 37 exempts the act from the tax-preference performance-statement/JLARC automatic-review requirements (RCW 82.32.805/.808), even though Sec. 36 touches a property-tax exemption (RCW 84.39.020) for veterans' widows — a drafting choice that avoids future sunset review of that tax provision.

Sections 24-27 (armed-forces, Purple Heart, and Pearl Harbor license plates, and veterans emblems) get a staggered April 1, 2025 contingent effective/expiration date decoupled from the rest of the act, apparently for DOL system lead time; RCW 41.40.170's retroactive-recalculation note (from a prior 2023 act, not this bill) continues to reference the older, narrower veteran definition since 41.40.170 was excluded from the broadened standard.
deep_oneLine: 2SHB 2014 broadens Washington's statutory definition of "veteran" to reach general-under-honorable, other-than-honorable-with-VA-benefits, and LGBTQ+ bias discharges across dozens of licensing, tuition, employment, and benefit statutes, but deliberately excludes PERS and old-law police/fire pension military service credit from that broadened standard, and makes the entire act null and void absent a 2024 appropriation.

brief: Concerning flexible work policies for law enforcement officers and participation in the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system plan 2.
haiku_summary: The bill expands eligibility for the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system (LEOFF) to include part-time law enforcement officers employed on a fully compensated basis.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 49.28 RCW authorizing (not requiring) general and limited authority Washington law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies, subject to no displacement of full-time officers, no alteration of existing collective bargaining agreements or duty-to-bargain obligations, and a requirement that full-time and part-time officers in the same bargaining unit be covered together.

Strikes the 'full-time,' qualifier from the definitions of 'general authority Washington peace officer' and 'limited authority Washington peace officer,' extending those statuses (used for mutual aid and commissioning purposes) to part-time commissioned officers.

In the pre-July 1, 2025 version of the LEOFF definitions section, strikes 'full time' from the city-police-officer qualifier and adds new subsection (19)(g) providing that 'law enforcement officer' does not include reserve peace officers called into active service under RCW 10.93.020.

Adds new subsection (19)(h) to the pre-July 1, 2025 version of RCW 41.26.030 making a person commissioned and fully compensated, but working less than full time, a 'law enforcement officer' eligible for LEOFF Plan 2 membership beginning July 1, 2024.

Makes the parallel amendment (reserve-officer exclusion at new (19)(g) and part-time officer inclusion at new (19)(h)) to the post-July 1, 2025 version of RCW 41.26.030, which already incorporates the 2023 c 77 tribal-police-officer membership provision, so the part-time definition carries forward without a gap.

Sunsets the temporary Section 3 version of RCW 41.26.030 on July 1, 2025, and makes the parallel Section 4 version effective the same date, synchronizing the part-time officer definition with the already-scheduled tribal officer amendment.

deep_whoAffected: Part-time (less-than-full-time), fully compensated commissioned peace officers of general and limited authority Washington law enforcement agencies gain LEOFF Plan 2 "law enforcement officer" eligibility; reserve peace officers called into active service are expressly excluded from LEOFF membership status.
deep_poi: The bill text contains no actuarial or fiscal adjustment language, yet it expands the LEOFF Plan 2 covered population to a new class of part-time officers; an OSA reader would look for the accompanying fiscal note rather than the bill itself for cost impact to the tri-party (state/employer/employee) funded plan.

The eligibility expansion is threaded twice, into both the pre- and post-July 1, 2025 versions of RCW 41.26.030 (Sec. 3 and Sec. 4), using an expire/take-effect pairing (Sec. 5, Sec. 6) to keep the temporary and permanent versions in sync with the already-scheduled 2023 c 77 tribal-officer amendment; any future drafter who amends only one version risks the two falling out of alignment.

The reserve-officer exclusion is a narrow carve-out drawn specifically to prevent reserve peace officers called into active duty under chapter 10.93 RCW from being swept into LEOFF membership by the new part-time officer language, forestalling an unintended eligibility expansion to a much larger and more casual class of personnel.

The flexible-work-policy authorization (Sec. 1, chapter 49.28 RCW) is a labor-policy provision layered loosely onto the pension eligibility change via a shared definitions cross-reference (RCW 10.93.020); an agency can adopt a flexible work policy without necessarily triggering the LEOFF membership question, and existing LEOFF Plan 2 service-credit tiers (70/90-hour monthly thresholds) already accommodate part-time work, so the practical benefit-computation mechanics for final average salary during transitions between full-time and part-time status are not separately addressed.
deep_oneLine: HB 2024 authorizes law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies for peace officers and, in the companion definitional amendments, opens LEOFF Plan 2 "law enforcement officer" membership to fully compensated but less-than-full-time officers beginning July 1, 2024, while expressly excluding reserve peace officers called into active service.

brief: Recognizing posttraumatic stress disorder as an occupational disease for county coroners, examiners, and investigative personnel.
triage_how: Expands workers' compensation occupational disease coverage for county coroners' PTSD without modifying pension benefits or eligibility.

hidden_how: Grepped the XML for retirement/pension/actuarial terms, then read the full text around each cluster (lines 442-450, 689-736, 775-791) to see whether the appropriations language changes benefits/contributions or merely funds routine actuarially-required contributions.

hidden_passages.where: Sec. 709 (lines 443-450), 'FOR THE DEPARTMENT OF RETIREMENT SYSTEMS—CONTRIBUTIONS TO RETIREMENT SYSTEMS'
hidden_passages.what: Standard omnibus-budget appropriation of state contributions to LEOFF, the judicial retirement system, and the judges' retirement system, with dollar figures revised upward (e.g., LEOFF total from $181.3M to $193.0M) per chapter 41.45 RCW and chapters 2.10/2.12 RCW schedules. This is the routine mechanism by which the state funds its actuarially required contribution each biennium; it does not change benefit levels, contribution rates, or plan rules.

hidden_passages.where: New Secs. 730-731 (lines 689-691), DRS 'PERS AND TRS PLAN 1 BENEFIT INCREASE' and 'DSHS COMPETENCY RESTORATION/PSERS' appropriations
hidden_passages.what: Appropriates funds ($ amounts per LEAP omnibus document, and $176,000) solely to cover the increased employer contribution rate that results if separate substantive bills (SHB 1985 PERS/TRS 1 benefit increase; HB 1949 DSHS competency restoration/PSERS) are enacted. Funding is contingent ("if the bill is not enacted... amounts shall lapse"); the budget bill itself does not create the benefit increase or PSERS coverage change, it only pre-funds the fiscal note of pending substantive legislation.

hidden_passages.where: Sec. 904 'COMPENSATION—PENSION CONTRIBUTIONS' (lines 783-791)
hidden_passages.what: Seven numbered provisos adjusting agency/school-district appropriations to match pension contribution rates set by the Pension Funding Council and the LEOFF Plan 2 Board, and funding specific rate increases (0.01%-0.23% of payroll across PERS, SERS, PSERS, TRS, WSPRS, LEOFF 2) tied to named substantive bills: SB 5350 (PERS 1/TRS 1 retiree benefit increase), SHB 1007 (military service credit), SHB 1056 (postretirement employment), chapter 199 Laws of 2023 (public safety telecommunicators/PSERS), HB 1949 (DSHS competency restoration/PSERS), and SHB 1985 (PERS/TRS 1 benefit increase). Each subsection is null and void, with appropriations held unallotted, if its companion bill is not enacted by a stated deadline.

hidden_passages.where: Line 64, health care authority/OST actuarial support proviso; lines 779, 781, actuarial-value language in school employees' benefits proviso
hidden_passages.what: 'Actuarial' appears in the context of health-benefits cost-sharing (actuarial value of health plans) and a directive for the health care authority to support the Office of the State Actuary with data for legislature's health care actuarial analysis — unrelated to pension policy.

hidden_poi: All pension-related sections are boilerplate budget-bill mechanics: they appropriate money to fund contribution-rate changes and benefit increases that were enacted (or contingently enacted) through separate, dedicated substantive bills (SB 5350, SHB 1985, SHB 1007, SHB 1056, HB 1949, ch. 199 Laws of 2023) — this bill does not itself create or amend any pension benefit, eligibility, or contribution-rate rule.

The 'null and void ... held in unallotted status' contingency clauses (Sec. 904 subsections 2-7) are the standard WA budget technique for making appropriations contingent on companion substantive legislation passing — not a hidden policy change, but worth flagging because it shows this budget bill is financially entangled with at least six separate pension bills from the 2023-24 biennium.

Sec. 709 and Secs. 730-731 revise dollar amounts for DRS contributions upward, consistent with normal biennial actuarial funding adjustments (LEOFF, judicial, judges' retirement systems) — no rate-suspension or funding-holiday language found anywhere in the bill.

No language found that suspends, defers, or reduces employer/employee contribution rates, changes vesting, or alters retirement benefit formulas directly within this bill — the 86 hits are essentially all appropriations-line and proviso boilerplate referencing pension systems by name.

brief: Concerning workers' compensation incentives to return to work.
triage_how: It addresses workers' compensation return-to-work incentives and vocational rehabilitation, not public retirement systems or benefits.

brief: Updating terminology related to criminal insanity and competency to stand trial.
haiku_summary: SHB 2152 is not a pension bill; it updates criminal justice terminology related to competency to stand trial and criminal insanity findings throughout the criminal code.

deep_provisions.detail: Renames "competency restoration services" to "restoration treatment services" within the PSERS Plan 2 "member" definition covering staff at state institutions who provide custody/security for offender, probationary, or patient populations, or perform those services; no change to which job classes or institutions qualify.

Uncodified savings clause states the act's terminology amendments are not intended to change the substantive meaning of the underlying concepts and do not alter the applicability or effect of prior case law on criminal insanity or inability to proceed to trial.

Sets a contingent effective date tying two unrelated civil-commitment definitions to a prior act's trigger; this contingency does not apply to the PSERS section (Sec. 39), which takes effect on the bill's normal effective date.

deep_whoAffected: PSERS Plan 2 members employed at DSHS/DCYF institutions (juvenile rehabilitation facilities, mental health hospitals, child study and treatment centers) whose duties include custody/security for patients undergoing what the statute now calls "restoration treatment" rather than "competency restoration"; the covered class of employees is unchanged.
deep_poi: Of 55 amended/reenacted sections, only one (RCW 41.37.010) touches a retirement statute; the PSERS classification rests entirely on a single incidental relabeling inside a criminal-justice terminology bill, not on any deliberate pension policy change.

The bill carries its own savings clause (Sec. 57) disclaiming substantive effect, which is unusually explicit reassurance for a bill coded as pension-related — useful for an analyst confirming zero actuarial or eligibility impact rather than inferring it from silence.

RCW 41.37.010 is amended "as amended by 2023 c 199 s 3," a very recent companion act (2023 telecommunicator PERS/PSERS expansion); layering a terminology-only edit on top of a just-enacted substantive amendment raises an ordinary but nontrivial code-reviser sequencing/publication risk.

No cost-shifting, contribution-rate, multiplier, or membership-count effect is created; this is the rare "pension bill" that an OSA fiscal note would properly score as zero fiscal impact despite touching an RCW that defines a covered retirement plan's membership.
deep_oneLine: SHB 2152 is a 55-section terminology overhaul of Washington's criminal-insanity and competency-to-stand-trial statutes (replacing "incompetent"/"competency" language with "unable to proceed to trial due to a mental health condition" and similar person-first phrasing); its only PSERS touchpoint is a nominal relabeling of "competency restoration services" to "restoration treatment services" within the RCW 41.37.010 Plan 2 membership definition, with an accompanying savings clause stating the act changes no substantive meaning.

brief: Concerning retirement benefit eligibility for law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system plan 2 retirees that separate from service and choose to work in eligible positions on a part-time basis.
haiku_summary: The bill permits LEOFF Plan 2 retirees to work part-time in law enforcement or firefighter positions for up to 1040 hours annually for three years following a six-month separation without suspension of retirement benefits.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (4) to RCW 41.26.500 allowing a LEOFF 2 retiree who has separated from service for six months or more to work in an eligible LEOFF position for up to 1040 hours per calendar year for up to three years without suspension of the monthly retirement allowance.
Retirees using the new part-time return-to-work window forgo any service credit or other accrual of retirement benefits for hours worked during that period.

The bill expressly states the expanded postretirement work eligibility is not a contractual right and may be repealed or modified by the legislature at any time, a non-vesting disclaimer aimed at avoiding contract-clause protection under state pension case law.

Adds new definition (29) "Separation from service," specifying it occurs only when a person has terminated all employment with an employer, and that a written or oral agreement to resume employment with the same employer defeats separation and may violate the bona fide separation rule in RCW 41.26.062.

Because RCW 41.26.030 is already scheduled to be amended by 2023 c 77 effective July 1, 2025 (adding tribal police department officers to the "law enforcement officer" definition), the bill amends both the pre- and post-July 1, 2025 versions of the section in parallel to keep the new "separation from service" definition and renumbering consistent across both.

Sections 4 and 5 sunset the pre-July 1, 2025 version of the definitions section (Section 1) and set the effective date of the post-July 1, 2025 version (Section 2) to July 1, 2025, matching the existing 2023 c 77 schedule.

deep_whoAffected: LEOFF Plan 2 retirees who separate from service for six months or more and their rehiring LEOFF employers; no change for LEOFF Plan 1 members or non-LEOFF retirement systems
deep_poi: The 1040-hour/three-year return-to-work window lets a retiree draw a full pension and a part-time LEOFF paycheck simultaneously; benefit-formula spiking is blocked by the service-credit forgo clause, but the policy still raises the classic double-dipping optics/cost question OSA typically flags even where the funding math is neutral.

The new 'separation from service' definition is deliberately cross-referenced to the pre-arranged-return prohibition in RCW 41.26.062, suggesting drafters are threading a six-month bright-line rule around an existing anti-collusion standard rather than replacing it; the interaction between the two provisions is left for DRS to administer.

The non-contractual-right disclaimer in new RCW 41.26.500(4)(c) is unusual and purposeful drafting, an explicit attempt to keep this benefit outside the vested-rights doctrine that has otherwise made Washington pension liberalizations hard to unwind.

The double amendment of RCW 41.26.030 (Sections 1 and 2, with Sections 4 and 5 as bridging sunset/effective-date sections) is a technical artifact of a second pending bill (2023 c 77) already scheduled to take effect July 1, 2025; it is clean drafting but signals the section is a live target for multiple bills in the same biennium.
deep_oneLine: HB 2167 lets LEOFF 2 retirees who have separated from service for six months or more return to part-time LEOFF officer/firefighter work (up to 1040 hours per year, for up to three years) without suspension of their retirement allowance, while forgoing further service credit, and adds a statutory definition of "separation from service" tied to the anti-collusion return-to-work rule in RCW 41.26.062.

brief: Changing the health insurance subsidy rate for retired state employees and retired or disabled school employees.

brief: Concerning vacation leave accrual for state employees.
haiku_summary: The bill increases vacation leave accrual for state employees from 240 to 280 hours while maintaining the 240-hour cap for leave amounts that count toward pension compensation calculations.

deep_provisions.detail: Raises the maximum accrual of unused vacation leave for state officers and employees from 240 to 280 hours, and correspondingly raises the cap that applies when leave use is deferred and extended by statement of necessity.

Conforms the alternative no-statement-of-necessity vacation accumulation method to the new 280-hour threshold (three references changed from 240 to 280 hours); leaves intact the existing rule that this alternative accumulation shall not increase a retirement allowance under any public retirement system.

Removes the cross-reference to RCW 43.01.044 and 43.01.041 in the PERS plan 1 definition of compensation earnable while leaving the exclusion of remuneration for unused annual leave in excess of 240 hours unchanged, meaning the compensation-earnable exclusion threshold was not raised to match the new 280-hour accrual cap.

Adds a new exclusion to the WSPRS plan 1 definition of pension-computable salary for lump sum payments for unused accumulated vacation or annual leave in excess of 240 hours (plus hours earned since the member's anniversary date), applicable only to members commissioned before July 1, 2001, a group whose salary definition previously did not exclude such payments unlike the two later-commissioned cohorts.

Makes numerous nonsubstantive numeral-style edits converting spelled-out numbers to digits (e.g., sixty to 60, twelve to 12, seventy to 70) throughout the PERS definitions section, with no effect on benefits.

deep_whoAffected: All state civil-service employees (higher vacation accrual cap); PERS plan 1 members and, narrowly, WSPRS plan 1 members commissioned before July 1, 2001 (pension compensation-definition conformance/anti-spiking fix)
deep_poi: The bill's operative policy change (240 to 280 hour vacation cap) sits in Title 43.01, a personnel statute; three of its four sections instead amend PERS and WSPRS compensation definitions purely to keep the larger leave balance from flowing into pension-computable pay, i.e., this is fundamentally an anti-spiking conforming bill riding alongside an HR leave-policy change.

Sec. 3 strips the RCW 43.01.044/.041 cross-reference from the PERS plan 1 compensation-earnable exclusion but leaves the numeric threshold at 240 hours rather than updating it to 280; still protective in effect (anything paid above 240 hours stays excluded), but the mismatch between the new 280-hour accrual cap and the still-240-hour compensation exclusion is a drafting artifact worth flagging.

Sec. 4 creates a genuinely narrow carve-out: the added salary exclusion applies only to WSPRS officers commissioned before July 1, 2001, a closed and shrinking cohort nearing or past retirement eligibility, apparently closing a gap because later-commissioned cohorts already had this exclusion in their salary definitions.

No emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause, and no contingent effective date appear anywhere in the bill, consistent with the drafters treating this as fiscally neutral -- the existing 'shall not result in any increase in a retirement allowance' savings clause in RCW 43.01.044(3) is left undisturbed.
deep_oneLine: HB 2246 raises the general state employee vacation-accrual cap from 240 to 280 hours (RCW 43.01.040/.044) and makes conforming amendments to PERS plan 1 and WSPRS plan 1 compensation definitions so the added leave does not translate into higher pension-computable pay, including a new anti-spiking exclusion for a narrow class of WSPRS officers commissioned before July 1, 2001.

brief: Concerning membership in the public employees' retirement system for certain part-time bus drivers employed full-time by the federal government.
haiku_summary: The bill exempts from PERS membership part-time bus drivers employed full-time by the federal government while working for public transportation benefit areas at naval shipyards.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds new membership exception (23): persons hired on or after the effective date, employed by a public transportation benefit area (RCW 36.57A.010) as part-time bus drivers serving naval shipyards, are excluded from mandatory PERS membership if they are simultaneously employed full-time by an employer of the federal government and making contributions to the federal employees' retirement system.

Technical conforming amendment splitting the reference to the former combined 'volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund' into the two separate funds created by 2023 c 73, with no substantive policy effect.
Technical renaming of the 'liquor control board' to the 'liquor and cannabis board' to conform to the 2015 rename, no substantive policy effect.

deep_whoAffected: A narrow class of part-time bus drivers for a public transportation benefit area serving naval shipyard routes who are also full-time federal government employees (e.g., federal civilian shipyard workers driving a shuttle route, likely Kitsap Transit serving Puget Sound Naval Shipyard) lose PERS membership eligibility for that part-time job; other listed exception classes are unaffected in substance.
deep_poi: The new provision is an exclusion from membership, not an expansion of access: it relieves the transit employer of PERS employer contributions for these part-time drivers, while the drivers forgo any PERS service credit for that job, in exchange for avoiding simultaneous participation in two retirement systems for overlapping employment.

The carve-out is unusually specific in both geography and employment structure (part-time bus driver, naval shipyard route, employer is a public transportation benefit area, employee also full-time federal and contributing to FERS), suggesting the bill was drafted to fit one identifiable real-world workforce (transit agency shuttle drivers serving a naval shipyard) rather than a general policy class.

No fiscal note language, actuarial impact statement, or SCPP analysis is present in the bill text itself; given the request-of-SCPP sponsorship, the class size is presumably small enough that any PERS trust fund impact would be treated as negligible, but that determination is not visible from the text.

Two unrelated technical/reviser cleanup edits (firefighters' fund split, liquor board rename) are bundled into the same amendatory section as the substantive change, typical drafting practice when reopening a frequently-amended RCW section but worth separating out when assessing what the bill actually does.
deep_oneLine: HB 2316 amends RCW 41.40.023 to add a new, narrow PERS membership exclusion for part-time bus drivers on naval-shipyard routes for a public transportation benefit area who are simultaneously full-time federal employees contributing to the federal retirement system, plus carries two unrelated technical conforming edits in the same section.

brief: Concerning employees of the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' plan 2 retirement board.
haiku_summary: The bill exempts employees of the LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board from state civil service classification and grants the board independent authority to set staff salaries with notice to state officials.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds employees of the LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board to the list of positions exempt from classified civil service coverage under the state civil service law.

Removes the existing requirement that LEOFF 2 board staff (other than the executive director) be state employees under Title 41 RCW, instead authorizing the board itself to set staff salaries subject to periodic board review.

Changes the process for setting the executive director's salary: the board must now merely provide notice to the OFM director rather than consult with OFM, while continuing to notify the house and senate fiscal committee chairs of changes.

deep_whoAffected: Staff and executive director of the LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board (a small administrative body), who gain hiring/compensation autonomy; OFM loses its consultative role over executive salary-setting.
deep_poi: The carve-out affects an extremely small class (the board's own staff, likely fewer than a dozen positions), the kind of narrow personnel-law exemption that draws little floor debate but sets durable precedent.

Removing the Title 41 RCW state-employee requirement lets the board hire and pay staff outside the classified civil service and general state salary schedules, mirroring autonomy already granted to entities like the state investment board; this is a governance template other retirement boards could later seek.

Downgrading OFM's role from 'consultation with' to 'notice to' on executive director salary-setting reduces centralized executive-branch oversight of compensation, shifting effective control to the board and legislative fiscal committees (notice only, not approval).

The bill is by request of the LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board itself, i.e., a governance/HR housekeeping measure originating from the board rather than OSA or SCPP, with no apparent fiscal note implications for plan funding, benefits, or contribution rates.
deep_oneLine: HB 2337 exempts LEOFF Plan 2 Retirement Board employees from civil service coverage and gives the board direct authority to hire staff outside Title 41 RCW and set their salaries, downgrading OFM's role from consultation to mere notice.

brief: Concerning the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system plan 2.
haiku_summary: The bill eliminates the statute of limitations for the special death benefit, expands firefighter and tribal law enforcement officer eligibility, assigns employer liability for overpayments from member information errors, and permits retroactive disability benefit reclassification for occupational diseases like posttraumatic stress disorder.

deep_provisions.detail: Eliminates the statute of limitations on the LEOFF special death benefit and requires L&I to redetermine eligibility for beneficiaries previously denied solely for missing that deadline, with an option to reelect an ongoing pension under RCW 41.26.510(2) paid retroactive to the member's death.

Expands the statutory definition of 'firefighter' to add full-time, fully compensated fire department personnel in positions that necessitate firefighter experience to perform essential job functions, with conforming subsection reletterings.

Makes the identical firefighter-definition addition to the parallel, later-effective version of the same definitions section that already incorporates the 2023 tribal-officer and general-authority-agency language, via a synchronized expiration/effective-date pair (Sec. 201 expires 7/1/2025; Sec. 202 takes effect 7/1/2025) so the change survives the scheduled 2023 c 77 amendment.

Provides that a LEOFF 2 retiree is not liable to repay a pension overpayment caused by an employer's erroneous reporting of member information (absent member nondisclosure, fraud, or misrepresentation), and exempts such employer-caused overpayments from the standard three-year lookback limit on benefit corrections.

Creates a new section making the employer liable to reimburse the LEOFF 2 retirement fund for overpayments caused by the employer's erroneous reporting, with liability capped at one year of overpayments plus interest unless the employer committed fraud, in which case the employer is liable for the full overpayment; effective January 1, 2025.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 41.26 RCW (Sec. 302); Sec. 303

deep_provisions.detail: Allows a member receiving a nonduty disability benefit for a condition not classified as an occupational disease at the time of retirement, but now meeting the PTSD occupational-disease definition, to file a new application for a line-of-duty disability determination, with the higher benefit paid retroactive to the date the condition became eligible as an occupational disease.

deep_whoAffected: LEOFF Plan 2 active members, retirees, beneficiaries, and their employers, with the death-benefit statute-of-limitations fix also reaching past-denied beneficiaries chapter-wide and a narrow class of nonduty PTSD disability retirees gaining a reclassification path
deep_poi: Sec. 101(3) reopens denied special-death-benefit claims with no dollar cap or outer time bound on the retroactive pension payments, creating open-ended liability exposure tied to a claims-processing failure rather than a benefit design change.

Sec. 302 is a cost-shift from members to employers for employer reporting errors, but the one-year cap (absent fraud) means older employer-caused overpayments still fall back on the fund/member, only partially transferring the liability.

Sec. 401(12) ties a retroactive disability-reclassification right to L&I's evolving occupational-disease determinations for PTSD, meaning future L&I policy changes could retroactively convert an unknown, currently-unquantifiable number of nonduty retirements into higher-cost line-of-duty retirements.

The twin-section drafting for RCW 41.26.030 (Secs. 201-204) is pension-code bookkeeping to synchronize with a previously enacted, not-yet-effective 2023 amendment rather than a substantive change in itself, and is easy to misread as two separate policy changes.
deep_oneLine: HB 2338 removes the statute of limitations on LEOFF special death benefit claims and creates a retroactive reopening path for previously denied beneficiaries, shifts liability for employer-caused LEOFF 2 pension overpayments from retirees to employers (capped at one year absent fraud), modestly broadens the firefighter definition, and lets certain nonduty PTSD disability retirees seek retroactive reclassification to line-of-duty status as L&I's occupational-disease determinations evolve.

brief: Establishing a state patrol longevity bonus.
haiku_summary: The bill establishes an annual $15,000 longevity bonus for Washington State Patrol commissioned employees with 26 or more years of service, excluding the bonus from pension benefit calculations.

deep_provisions.detail: Creates a new state trooper longevity bonus of $15,000 annually, paid on the employee's state-service anniversary date, for eligible commissioned employees with 26 or more years of service, beginning July 1, 2024.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(1), (6))

deep_provisions.detail: Establishment of the bonus is made subject to negotiated changes in the applicable collective bargaining agreements with the exclusive bargaining representatives, and the section expressly disclaims any interference with collective bargaining rights under RCW 41.56.473.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(2), (3)); RCW 41.56.473

deep_provisions.detail: Declares the bonus a time-limited incentive not intended to be included in salary or average final salary for pension benefit calculations, and states it is not a matter of contractual right, so the legislature may alter or abolish it at any time.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(4), (5))

deep_provisions.detail: The new bonus section itself expires June 30, 2029, sunsetting the pilot program.
deep_provisions.cites: New section added to chapter 43.43 RCW (Sec. 2(7))

deep_provisions.detail: Amends the WSPRS definition of 'salary' for all three commissioning-date tiers to expressly exclude earnings from the new longevity bonus, preventing the bonus from inflating average final salary and retirement allowances.

Converts several spelled-out numbers in the WSPRS definitions section (e.g., 'seventy' to '70,' 'sixty' to '60,' 'twelve' to '12,' 'seventy-seven' to '77') to numerals; a non-substantive drafting cleanup riding along with the salary amendment.
Section 3 (the RCW 43.43.120 amendment carrying the salary exclusion) is itself set to expire June 30, 2029, tying the salary-exclusion language to the same sunset as the bonus program.

Requires the joint legislative audit and review committee to complete a performance review of the longevity bonus pilot by November 1, 2028, assessing retention impact, vacancy trends, optimal staffing levels compared to other states, and other retention factors, and to recommend whether to continue the program; this review section also expires June 30, 2029.

deep_whoAffected: Washington State Patrol commissioned employees (troopers/sergeants) in the Washington State Patrol Retirement System with 26 or more years of service; no other WSPRS members or classes are affected.
deep_poi: The bonus is deliberately walled off from pension calculations: Sec. 2(4) and the parallel amendments to the 'salary' definition in RCW 43.43.120(21)(a)-(c) both exclude the $15,000 payment from average final salary, an explicit anti-spiking design choice for what is otherwise a large annual payment to a senior, near-retirement cohort.

The entire program is a five-year pilot: the new benefit section, the salary-exclusion amendment (via a separate standalone Sec. 5 expiration section), and the JLARC review mandate all sunset June 30, 2029, with the review due by November 1, 2028 to inform a continuation decision.

Eligibility is unusually narrow and senior: 26+ years of service (beyond the roughly 25-year mark the findings cite for 122 currently retirement-eligible staff), targeting retention of the most senior commissioned staff specifically to preserve a leadership pipeline, rather than addressing broader recruitment or mid-career retention.

The bonus's actual establishment is made contingent on collective bargaining agreement changes (Sec. 2(2)), and the bill preserves the legislature's unilateral right to alter or abolish it (Sec. 2(5)) with no contractual right created, standard non-vesting boilerplate that keeps this off the books as a pension enhancement despite its size and recurrence.
deep_oneLine: Creates a time-limited (through June 30, 2029) $15,000 annual longevity bonus for Washington State Patrol commissioned employees with 26+ years of service, statutorily excluded from salary and average final salary for pension calculation purposes, contingent on collective bargaining agreement changes, with a mandated 2028 JLARC performance review.

brief: Concerning sustainability factors in investment strategies and proxy voting by the Washington state investment board.
haiku_summary: The bill requires the Washington State Investment Board to integrate sustainability and climate risk factors into investment decision-making, portfolio management, and proxy voting governance.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds subsection requiring the board to integrate sustainability factors (governance, environmental, social, human capital) into its investment decision making, analysis, portfolio construction, due diligence, and ownership when determining a prudent level of risk.

Enumerates a non-exhaustive list of sustainability factors the board should strive to incorporate when updating sustainability frameworks, covering corporate governance/leadership, environmental, social capital, human capital, and business model/innovation categories.

Adds a new duty for the board to develop and publish proxy voting guidelines treating climate change as a business and systemic risk, support shareholder resolutions reducing climate-change-contributing activity, and publicly justify in writing any decision not to support such resolutions.

Adds a new annual reporting requirement on the environmental sustainability of the board's investment decision-making process, including climate-related risk identification, financial impact assessment, and mitigation actions tied to federal climate-related reporting requirements.

Creates a new section directing the state auditor to conduct a biennial (starting December 1, 2027) evaluation of WSIB's climate-risk proxy voting guidelines and conformance, reporting findings and recommendations to the legislature.

deep_whoAffected: No member class gains or loses benefits; the bill governs WSIB's investment and proxy-voting practices, indirectly affecting all beneficiaries of the pension funds and other public funds WSIB manages as fiduciary assets.
deep_poi: This is not a benefits bill: it contains no multiplier, COLA, contribution, or eligibility change; it regulates WSIB's fiduciary investment and proxy-voting process, which is unusual for a bill classified as pension-related.

The bill layers a policy mandate (climate-risk-focused sustainability integration and proxy voting) onto WSIB's existing prudent-investor standard in RCW 43.33A.140, raising a potential tension between the statutory duty to maximize return at prudent risk and a directive to support climate-related shareholder resolutions, which analysts often flag as a fiduciary-duty overlay question even though the bill frames sustainability factors as return-maximizing.

The bill creates an external oversight mechanism (state auditor biennial review of proxy voting conformance, first due December 1, 2027) rather than legislature-facing SCPP oversight, a structurally different accountability channel than typical pension bills.

No fiscal note mechanics are present in the text itself (no appropriation language, no actuarial funding note, no contingent effective date, no emergency clause), consistent with a governance/process bill rather than a benefit-cost bill.
deep_oneLine: HB 2405 directs WSIB to integrate climate and other sustainability factors into investment decision-making, adopt proxy voting guidelines favoring climate-risk-reducing shareholder resolutions, report annually on environmental sustainability of its investment process, and requires a state auditor evaluation of proxy voting conformance every two years starting December 2027.

hidden_passages.what: The bill must reenact RCW 43.84.092 three times because that statute currently exists in three parallel effective-date versions (a quirk of multiple uncoordinated 2023 session laws amending it without reference to one another, per the reviser's note at line 38). Each version contains the identical giant boilerplate list of ~140 state treasury accounts and funds that receive a proportionate share of pooled investment earnings. The bill's only edit to this list is inserting one new entry: 'the development of renewable energy for Washington revolving loan account.' The list, unchanged apart from that insertion, happens to include: the deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts, the department of retirement systems expense account, the higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund, the judges'/judicial retirement accounts, the pension funding stabilization account, the PERS plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, the reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, the supplemental pension account, the TRS plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, the Washington judicial retirement system account, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, the Washington public safety employees' plan 2 account, the school employees' retirement system combined plan 2/3 account, the Washington state patrol retirement account, and the money-purchase retirement savings accounts. None of these entries' treatment is altered; they are simply carried forward verbatim in the reenacted list, which is why each pension-related account name shows up three times (once per reenacted version), accounting for the bulk of the 39 term hits.

hidden_poi: All 39 pension-term hits trace to a single recurring boilerplate list of treasury accounts in RCW 43.84.092, repeated three times because the bill must reenact three parallel effective-date versions of that statute (a housekeeping consequence of multiple 2023 session laws that amended RCW 43.84.092 without referencing each other).

The bill's only actual edit to that list is adding one new line item, the renewable energy revolving loan account, so it can also receive its share of state treasury pooled investment earnings, consistent with how dozens of other unrelated program accounts (retirement and non-retirement alike) are treated.

No contribution rate, benefit formula, actuarial assumption, or funding-method provision for PERS, TRS, LEOFF, SERS, PSERS, WSPRS, or judicial retirement is touched. This is not a pension proviso riding an omnibus bill; it is mechanical inclusion of pension accounts in a routine investment-earnings allocation statute that the bill amends for an unrelated reason.

General flag for future bills of this type: any bill that reenacts RCW 43.84.092 (or its sibling RCW 43.79A.040, which contains a similar list and shows up at the very start of the file's account list) will trigger high pension-term counts purely from the boilerplate account list, not from substantive pension policy. Worth excluding these two RCW sections from term-count-based pension flagging or treating hits confined to them as low priority.

triage_how: SHB 2437 establishes a task force to study private sector retirement savings programs for Washington businesses, not public retirement systems, and makes no changes to public pension law or benefits.

brief: Increasing defined benefit accrual for specified years of service in the state retirement systems.
haiku_summary: The bill increases the defined benefit accrual rate by one-half percent per year for each year of service beyond 30 years in PERS, SERS, and TRS.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds a new bonus accrual of an additional 0.5% of average final compensation per year of service beyond 30 years, for TRS 2 members, applicable only to years of service earned after the section's effective date.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for TRS 3 members' defined benefit portion, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for SERS 2 members, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for SERS 3 members' defined benefit portion, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for PERS 2 members, prospective only.
Adds the same 0.5%-per-year-beyond-30-years bonus accrual for PERS 3 members' defined benefit portion, prospective only.

deep_whoAffected: Active PERS 2/3, SERS 2/3, and TRS 2/3 members who work beyond 30 years of service credit; no effect on members who separate at or before 30 years, and no retroactive effect on years already earned.
deep_poi: The bonus applies only to years of service earned after the bill's effective date, so a member with 32 years at enactment gets the enhanced 2.5% rate only on future years beyond 30, not on the two years already worked past the 30-year mark; this creates a mixed-formula calculation for long-tenure members mid-career.

Benefit is narrowly targeted at a small population of very long-tenured members (30+ years of service), which in PERS/SERS/TRS Plan 2/3 is a relatively small share of the active membership, concentrating fiscal cost on a specific late-career cohort.

Uniform 0.5% bump is applied identically across six sections/three systems/two plan designs (Plan 2 and the DB half of Plan 3) rather than being tailored to each system's differing normal cost or funded status, suggesting a policy-driven rather than actuarially-calibrated design choice.

No emergency clause, no null-and-void-without-appropriation clause, and no contingent effective date appear in the bill text, meaning it would take effect under the standard 90-days-after-sine-die rule absent a fiscal note constraint added later; this leaves cost absorption to the standard PERS/SERS/TRS contribution rate-setting process rather than tying implementation to appropriated funding.
deep_oneLine: HB 2471 adds a 0.5% per-year multiplier bonus for service beyond 30 years, prospectively, across the Plan 2 benefit formulas of TRS, SERS, and PERS.

brief: Making 2023-2025 fiscal biennium operating appropriations and 2021-2023 fiscal biennium second supplemental operating appropriations.
haiku_summary: ESSB 5187 is the 2023-2025 biennium operating appropriations bill and does not substantively change any public retirement system policies or benefits.

deep_provisions.detail: Extends into the 2023-2025 fiscal biennium the existing requirement that port districts and institutions of higher education pay both the employer and state pension contribution shares for LEOFF 2 members who are law enforcement officers or firefighters performing fee-for-service work for entities that are not their statutory 'employer'.

Funds a 0.12 percent increase in PERS, PSERS, and SERS employer contributions and a 0.23 percent increase in TRS employer contributions to pay for a one-time ongoing benefit increase for PERS 1 and TRS 1 retirees; the subsection is null and void, and the appropriations held in unallotted status, if Senate Bill No. 5350 is not enacted by June 30, 2023.

Funds a 0.13 percent increase in Washington state patrol retirement system employer contributions and a 0.01 percent increase in LEOFF 2 employer contributions to fund a military service credit purchase benefit; null and void if Senate Bill No. 5296 is not enacted by June 30, 2023.

Appropriates $181.3 million (biennium) in state contributions to LEOFF, made monthly per chapter 41.45 RCW, plus $12.3 million to the judicial retirement system and $600,000 to the judges' retirement system, made quarterly per chapters 2.10 and 2.12 RCW, and $18.704 million to the volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension fund.

Appropriates $34.491 million (2023-25) and $6.007 million (2021-23 supplemental) to the Department of Retirement Systems for 'pension system modernization,' subject to the IT-project oversight conditions of Sec. 701, plus smaller sums contingent on enactment of companion pension bills, including SB 5296 (military service credit, $143,000), SSB 5538 (postretirement nursing, $1,172,000), SB 5084 (self-insured pensions/fund, $41,000 plus $84,000/$84,000 from L&I accident and medical aid accounts), SB 5367 (inactive retirement accounts, $619,000), SB 5021 ($286,000), and ESSB 5399 (universal health care commission, $7,000); two supplemental items for SB 5676 (PERS/TRS 1 benefit increase, $48,000) and HB 1669 (PSERS disability benefits, $82,000) carry a June 30, 2022 enactment deadline that had already passed, so those amounts lapse.

Nearly every pension item in this budget is a funding pass-through rather than a benefit change: contribution-rate bumps and DRS implementation costs for SB 5350, SB 5296, SB 5084, SB 5538, SB 5367, SB 5676, and HB 1669 are all null and void (appropriations unallotted) if those freestanding bills fail to pass -- the actual benefit design sits entirely outside this text.

The one direct LEOFF 2 statutory change (RCW 41.26.450) is a narrow anti-subsidy/cost-shifting mechanic, not a benefit change: it makes port districts and higher-ed institutions absorb both employer and state contribution shares when their LEOFF 2 officers or firefighters do outside fee-for-service work, preventing the state general fund from indirectly subsidizing third-party service arrangements.

The military-service-credit and PERS1/TRS1 benefit-increase funding is expressed as small employer contribution-rate increments (0.01%-0.23%) layered onto rates already set by the Pension Funding Council and the LEOFF 2 board and adjusted under SB 5294 (plan 1 UAAL rates), typical incremental normal-cost/UAAL funding mechanics rather than a rate-setting policy change in its own right.
