Analysts scanning for hidden pension provisos in appropriations/omnibus bills should note this pattern (RCW 43.84.092 amendments) as a common source of false-positive pension term matches -- worth excluding or down-weighting in future automated scans.

brief: Concerning actuarial funding of state retirement systems.
haiku_summary: The bill establishes a declining schedule of employer contribution rates through June 2027 for funding unfunded actuarial liabilities in state retirement plans, with a 0.50 percent minimum thereafter.

deep_provisions.detail: Caps the existing 3.50 percent minimum PERS/PSERS employer contribution rate for amortizing PERS Plan 1 unfunded actuarial accrued liability (UAAL) so it runs only through June 30, 2023, deleting the prior open-ended duration of 'until the actuarial value of assets ... equals 100 percent.'
Caps the existing 3.50 percent minimum SERS employer contribution rate for the same PERS Plan 1 UAAL so it runs only through August 31, 2023, removing the same open-ended 100 percent funded trigger.
Caps the existing 5.75 percent minimum TRS employer contribution rate for TRS Plan 1 UAAL so it runs only through August 31, 2023, removing the same open-ended trigger.

Establishes a new declining employer contribution rate schedule for PERS/PSERS (2.50%, 2.00%, 1.50%, 0.50% for fiscal years 2024-2027) dedicated to PERS Plan 1 UAAL, followed by a 0.50 percent minimum floor beginning July 1, 2027 that applies only while plan assets are below 100 percent of accrued liability.

Establishes the identical declining schedule (2.50% down to 0.50%, fiscal years 2024-2027) for SERS employer rates dedicated to PERS Plan 1 UAAL, followed by the same funding-contingent 0.50 percent floor beginning September 1, 2027.

Establishes a declining schedule for TRS employer rates dedicated to TRS Plan 1 UAAL running from 0.50 percent (FY2024-25) down to 0.00 percent (FY2026-27), followed by the same funding-contingent 0.50 percent floor beginning September 1, 2027.

Adds a new subsection directing the state actuary, upon completion of each biennial actuarial valuation, to review the minimum contribution rates and recommend adjustments to the Pension Funding Council for material changes in benefits, assumptions, methods, or experience, with any council changes subject to legislative revision.

Reduces the one-time fiscal year 2023 General Fund-State appropriation for deposit into the TRS Plan 1 fund (to be applied against the plan's unfunded actuarial accrued liability on June 30, 2023) from $800,000,000 to $250,000,000.
Declares an emergency for immediate preservation of public peace, health, safety, or state government operations, and sets the act's effective date as June 30, 2023.

deep_whoAffected: Public employers in PERS/PSERS, SERS, and TRS (who pay the amortization-rate share of employer contributions) and the state general fund, not individual member benefits; PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 legacy funding levels are affected indirectly
deep_poi: Section 2 cuts the FY2023 supplemental general-fund deposit into the TRS Plan 1 fund from $800 million to $250 million, a $550 million reduction in one-time UAAL paydown, timed to an effective date of June 30, 2023 (the last day of that fiscal year) under an emergency clause, meaning the reduced appropriation takes effect essentially concurrent with the close of the fiscal year it governs.

The bill swaps an indefinite 'minimum rate until 100 percent funded' floor for a fixed, declining stairstep schedule that sunsets in 2027, then reinstates a minimum rate only conditioned on funded status (below 100 percent) rather than a hard date - a shift from open-ended to time-boxed-plus-contingent design that could affect long-run amortization certainty.

The TRS schedule glides to a 0.00 percent employer rate by FY2026-2027 while the PERS/PSERS and SERS schedules bottom out at 0.50 percent, implying TRS Plan 1 is assumed to reach full funding on a faster track than PERS Plan 1 - worth checking against the underlying OSA valuation assumptions.

New subsection (7) creates a recurring state actuary review-and-recommend loop to the Pension Funding Council each biennial valuation, institutionalizing periodic rate reassessment rather than leaving the schedule static through 2027 as enacted.
deep_oneLine: ESSB 5294 replaces the open-ended minimum employer contribution rates for PERS/PSERS, SERS, and TRS Plan 1 unfunded liability with a declining rate schedule running through fiscal year 2027 (backstopped by a funding-contingent 0.50 percent floor thereafter), adds a state actuary review-and-recommend requirement, and cuts the fiscal year 2023 one-time general fund deposit to the TRS Plan 1 fund from $800 million to $250 million, effective immediately under an emergency clause.

hidden_how: Grepped the bill text for pension-related terms, then diffed the two near-identical occurrences of the treasury income account list (RCW 43.84.092) to confirm the retirement-related entries are unchanged boilerplate, not amended provisions.

hidden_passages.where: Two near-duplicate sections amending RCW 43.84.092, 'Treasury income account—Accounts and funds credited' (one current, one effective-date-triggered version dated July 1, 2024), appearing roughly at file offsets 6500-13900 and 54000-61000
hidden_passages.what: Both sections contain the same long enumerated list of ~150 state accounts and funds entitled to a proportionate share of treasury income account earnings. Embedded in that list are references to: the department of retirement systems expense account, the pension funding stabilization account, the public employees' retirement system plan 1 account, the public employees' retirement system combined plan 2 and 3 account, the supplemental pension account, the teachers' retirement system plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, the volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, the Washington judicial retirement system account, the Washington law enforcement officers' and firefighters' system plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, the Washington public safety employees' plan 2 retirement account, the Washington school employees' retirement system combined plan 2/3 account, the Washington state patrol retirement account, and the deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts.

hidden_passages.where: Diff between the two occurrences of the account list
hidden_passages.what: The only substantive difference between the two versions of the list is the removal of 'the ambulance transport fund' from the enumerated accounts (consistent with the bill's short title, 'Eliminating accounts'). Every retirement-, pension-, and deferred-compensation-related account name is present, in the same form, in both the pre- and post-amendment text — none of them is added, removed, or otherwise altered.

hidden_poi: All 24+ pension-related hits come from a single recurring statutory boilerplate list (RCW 43.84.092) of accounts that share pro rata investment earnings from the state treasury income account — not from any pension policy section.

The bill's actual operative change is narrow: it deletes 'the ambulance transport fund' (and similarly trims a couple of other non-pension accounts, e.g. related to Western Washington University/Yakima integrated plan implementation accounts appear to be cut in a later, unrelated section of the bill) from the RCW 43.84.092 earnings-distribution list — nothing pension-related is added or removed.
No LEOFF-specific provisions, no actuarial references, no contribution-rate language, and no benefit or funding-formula changes appear anywhere in the bill text.

This is a textbook case of retirement-system account names appearing only because bills that amend the treasury income account statute must restate the entire long list verbatim (WA drafting convention); it should not be reclassified as pension-adjacent legislation.

brief: Concerning interruptive military service credit for members of the state retirement systems.
triage_how: It amends the definition of veteran in RCW 41.04.005 to expand eligibility for military service credit in the state retirement systems by clarifying that expeditionary medals qualify alongside campaign medals.

brief: Defining attending provider and clarifying other provider functions for workers' compensation claims, and adding psychologists as attending providers for mental health only claims.
triage_how: Bill regulates health care providers in the workers' compensation system, which is separate from and does not affect public employee retirement systems.

hidden_how: All 24 pension-term hits fall inside the same boilerplate RCW 43.84.092 account-list, amended only to insert a new 'electric-assisted bicycle account' alongside pre-existing entries, with no change to any retirement system's benefits, contributions, or funding.

hidden_passages.where: Sec. 5 (RCW 43.84.092, effective until 7/1/2024), line 71
hidden_passages.what: Long alphabetized list of treasury accounts/funds that receive proportionate investment earnings; includes PERS plan 1 account, PERS combined plan 2/3 account, TRS plan 1 account, TRS combined plan 2/3 account, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 accounts, WA public safety employees' plan 2 account, WA school employees' retirement combined plan 2/3 account, WA state patrol retirement account, judges'/judicial retirement accounts, deferred compensation admin/principal accounts, pension funding stabilization account, supplemental pension account, volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension fund, higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund, and department of retirement systems expense account. The amendment's only substantive change is inserting 'the electric-assisted bicycle account' into this pre-existing list.

hidden_passages.where: Sec. 6 (RCW 43.84.092, effective 7/1/2024), line 217
hidden_passages.what: Identical boilerplate account list (the post-7/1/2024 version of the same statute, amended in parallel), again with the sole substantive edit being addition of the electric-assisted bicycle account to the enumeration.

hidden_poi: This is the standard mechanism by which any bill creating a new state treasury account picks up dozens of pension-term hits: RCW 43.84.092 lists every account entitled to a share of treasury income account earnings, and nearly all state retirement system accounts are on that list by default.

No contribution rates, benefit formulas, actuarial assumptions, or DRS administrative authority are touched; the retirement-related account names are unmodified copy carried forward from the existing statute.

Because RCW 43.84.092 is amended twice in the same bill (a pre- and post-7/1/2024 version, both keyed to prior 2022 c 182 amendments), the same boilerplate list appears twice, doubling the raw term count without doubling the substance.

This pattern (false positive from RCW 43.84.092 boilerplate) is likely to recur across many unrelated bills that create new special accounts and should probably be filtered out or down-weighted in any automated pension-bill classifier.

brief: Concerning public safety employees' retirement plan membership for public safety telecommunicators.
haiku_summary: The bill establishes Public Safety Employees' Retirement System membership eligibility for 911 emergency dispatchers and telecommunicators employed by public employers.

deep_provisions.detail: Expands the RCW 41.37.010(12) definition of 'employer' to include any PERS-participating employer whose employees' primary responsibility is to receive, process, transmit, or dispatch 911 emergency and nonemergency calls, bringing those employers into PSERS coverage for that class of worker.

Adds a new RCW 41.37.010(19)(f) category to the definition of 'member,' extending PSERS eligibility to employees whose primary responsibility is to receive, process, transmit, or dispatch 911 emergency/nonemergency calls or to supervise such employees, plus a renumbered (g) for supervisors of newly eligible members.

Adds 'or psychological' to the legislative intent language in RCW 41.37.005 describing the physical risk that justifies separate PSERS treatment, textually extending the stated rationale for PSERS membership to psychological as well as physical occupational risk.

New section creates a one-time election period (January 1, 2024 through March 1, 2024) during which existing PERS Plan 2/3 telecommunicators employed as of June 1, 2024 may elect to become PSERS Plan 2 dual members under chapter 41.54 RCW, with membership effective prospectively from the election date and no transfer of accrued PERS service credit into PSERS.
deep_provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.37 RCW (Sec. 4); ch. 41.54 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: Telecommunicators who do not affirmatively elect to join PSERS by September 1, 2024 default to remaining in their current PERS plan, and PERS Plan 1 telecommunicators (members on or before June 1, 2019) are barred from switching and must remain in PERS Plan 1.
deep_provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.37 RCW (Sec. 4)

deep_provisions.detail: All newly hired telecommunicators meeting the eligibility definition who are hired on or after June 1, 2024 become PSERS members automatically, with no election required.
deep_provisions.cites: new section added to chapter 41.37 RCW (Sec. 4)

deep_whoAffected: Public safety telecommunicators (911 dispatchers/call-takers and their direct supervisors) employed by PERS-participating employers gain PSERS Plan 2 eligibility; PERS Plan 1 telecommunicators are excluded and remain in Plan 1; contract, nonprofit, and first-class-city telecommunicator employees are excluded entirely.
deep_poi: Section 1 is an unusual freestanding intent section that affirmatively narrows the bill's reach, explicitly disclaiming coverage for contract employees, nonprofit employees, and employees of first-class cities even though those entities may employ functionally identical telecommunicators; this creates a durable coverage gap that tracks employer type rather than job duties.

The election design (prospective-only join, no PERS service credit transfer into PSERS) avoids any actuarial cost of purchasing past service at PSERS rates, which limits the cost-shift to employers/plan compared to a full transfer-in design, but leaves electing members' PSERS benefit accrual starting from zero regardless of tenure.

The PERS Plan 1 carve-out (Sec. 4(5)) is a narrow, closed class: only those who were PERS 1 members on or before June 1, 2019 and remain PERS-covered telecommunicators past June 1, 2024. Because PERS 1 is closed and typically older/near-retirement, this avoids disrupting Plan 1's distinct benefit formula and funding status.

The 'or psychological' addition to the RCW 41.37.005 intent language is a small textual change but is notable because it is the only substantive amendment to the general PSERS rationale section, and could be read as legislative acknowledgment that psychological risk alone can justify PSERS-equivalent treatment for other occupational classes beyond telecommunicators.
deep_oneLine: SB 5328 adds public safety telecommunicators (911 dispatchers) employed by PERS-covered employers to PSERS Plan 2 membership, gives existing PERS 2/3 telecommunicators a one-time election window to transfer prospectively as dual members, locks in PERS 1 telecommunicators, and makes new hires after June 1, 2024 automatic PSERS members.

brief: Repealing some postretirement employment restrictions.
haiku_summary: The bill allows retirees under alternate early retirement provisions to work up to 867 hours annually without suspension of pension benefits, effective January 1, 2024.

deep_provisions.detail: Removes, effective January 1, 2024, the prior rule barring alternate early retirees (30 service years, age 55, benefit reduced per statutory schedule) from any postretirement employment until age 65, and instead lets them work up to 867 hours per calendar year under the standard postretirement employment provisions before reaching 65; the pre-2024 bar remains in force through December 31, 2023.

Broadens the definition of 'employment with an employer' for these alternate early retirees before age 65 to include personal service contracts and service as a temporary or project employee, then narrows it after age 65 to only the statutory 'employer' definition, changing what counts against the hours cap depending on the retiree's age.

Repeals a narrower, now-redundant subsection that had separately authorized up to 867 hours of postretirement work without benefit suspension for alternate early retirees who reentered nonadministrative employment after June 9, 2016, since the same 867-hour allowance is now granted directly in the eligibility sections; remaining subsections are relettered accordingly.

deep_whoAffected: TRS 2/3, SERS 2/3, and PERS 2/3 members who retired (or will retire) under the 30-service-year/age-55 'alternate early retirement' option, a narrower subset of the general early-retiree population
deep_poi: The bill's substantive reach is confined to one narrow retiree subclass, alternate early retirees who elected the 30-year/age-55 reduced-benefit path, even though it amends nine sections across three systems' plan 2/3 structures.

It liberalizes postretirement work rules by removing an age-65 employment bar that had specifically targeted this subclass, raising the usual return-to-work/benefit-suspension policy tension (workforce retention and staffing shortages, particularly in schools, versus double-dipping and cost-shifting concerns) without any accompanying fiscal note or study language in the bill text itself.

The employment definition is widened (capturing personal service contracts and temp/project work) for retirees under 65 but narrowed for retirees over 65 in the same sentence, an asymmetric anti-loophole drafting choice whose practical effect is muted by the fact that the underlying hours-limit prohibition it guards is being lifted at the same time.

The repealed carve-out in the reemployment sections overlapped with still-active, separately sunsetting (July 1, 2025) COVID-era school-district reemployment relief enacted by 2022 c 110, so this bill is layered on top of an already temporary, staggered set of postretirement employment rules rather than a clean baseline.
deep_oneLine: SB 5349 lifts the age-65 postretirement-employment bar for TRS 2/3, SERS 2/3, and PERS 2/3 members who retired under the 30-year/age-55 'alternate early retirement' option, letting them work up to 867 hours a year starting January 1, 2024, while consolidating and repealing a redundant narrower carve-out that previously served the same purpose.

brief: Providing a benefit increase to certain retirees of the public employees' retirement system plan 1 and the teachers' retirement system plan 1.
haiku_summary: The bill provides a one-time three percent cost-of-living adjustment capped at $110 monthly to current beneficiaries of PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 effective July 1, 2023.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds a fourth-tier one-time benefit increase for TRS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2022, effective July 1, 2023: 3 percent of the monthly benefit, capped at $110.00.

Adds a matching fourth-tier one-time benefit increase for PERS Plan 1 beneficiaries receiving a monthly benefit on July 1, 2022, effective July 1, 2023: 3 percent of the monthly benefit, capped at $110.00.
Excludes TRS 1 beneficiaries receiving benefits under the survivor/disability provisions of RCW 41.32.489 or 41.32.540 from the increase in this section.
Excludes PERS 1 beneficiaries receiving benefits under RCW 41.40.1984 from the increase in this section.
Restates the prior three tiers' dollar caps in numeral form ($62.50, $62.50, $110.00) rather than spelled-out text, a non-substantive drafting cleanup.
Uncodified legislative finding states that an ongoing COLA for PERS 1/TRS 1 beneficiaries may not be affordable until required employer UAAL contribution rates are reduced or eliminated.

Directs SCPP, during the 2023-2025 fiscal biennium, to study and recommend an ongoing COLA for PERS 1/TRS 1 beneficiaries, with any recommendation to consider employer contribution rate stability and to coordinate the COLA's effective date with reduction or elimination of the unfunded actuarial accrued liability.

deep_whoAffected: PERS Plan 1 and TRS Plan 1 retirees/beneficiaries on the benefit rolls as of July 1, 2022, excluding those drawing survivor or disability benefits under RCW 41.32.489, 41.32.540, or 41.40.1984
deep_poi: This is the fourth successive one-time, capped-dollar COLA layered onto the same two statutes (2018, 2020, 2022, now 2023) rather than a permanent indexed COLA; the ad hoc pattern itself is the policy, not a one-off fix.

Section 2 explicitly conditions any future ongoing COLA on reduction or elimination of the UAAL, an unusual instance of the legislature pre-committing a benefit study's scope to employer cost sequencing rather than beneficiary need.

The survivor/disability carve-outs under RCW 41.32.489/41.32.540 and 41.40.1984 have been excluded from every iteration of this ad hoc COLA since 2018; the bill perpetuates rather than revisits that exclusion, worth flagging for equity review.

An emergency clause is used for what is functionally a routine, incremental benefit bump rather than a genuine peace/health/safety measure; its practical effect is to move the effective date up and to place the act beyond referendum.
deep_oneLine: SB 5350 grants a one-time 3 percent COLA, capped at $110 a month, to PERS 1 and TRS 1 retirees on the rolls as of July 1, 2022, excludes certain survivor and disability beneficiaries from that increase, and directs the Select Committee on Pension Policy to study an ongoing COLA tied to paydown of the plans' unfunded liability, effective immediately under an emergency clause.

brief: Expanding access to the workers' compensation stay-at-work program through off-site light duty return to work opportunities.
triage_how: This bill concerns only workers' compensation benefits and return-to-work programs under the Department of Labor and Industries, not public retirement systems.

brief: Concerning participating in insurance plans and contracts by separated plan 2 members of certain retirement systems.
triage_how: The bill expands eligibility for post-employment health insurance coverage to separated Plan 2 members of three Washington retirement systems who are age 55 or older with at least 20 years of service.

brief: Concerning flexible work for general and limited authority Washington peace officers.
haiku_summary: The bill extends Law Enforcement Officers' and Firefighters' Retirement System membership eligibility to part-time law enforcement officers and firefighters who are fully compensated, effective July 1, 2024.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds a new section to chapter 49.28 RCW authorizing general and limited authority Washington law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible work policies (part-time work, alternative shifts), with guardrails barring displacement of full-time officers and preserving collective bargaining obligations and existing bargaining units.

Reenacts and amends the chapter 10.93 RCW definitions of "general authority Washington peace officer" and "limited authority Washington peace officer" by striking the existing "full-time" qualifier, so part-time commissioned officers now qualify as peace officers under that chapter.

Amends the currently effective version of the LEOFF definitions section to add a new law enforcement officer category, effective July 1, 2024, covering commissioned, fully compensated officers working less than full time who otherwise meet the existing qualifications, making them LEOFF Plan 2 members.

Makes the identical part-time officer eligibility addition to the version of RCW 41.26.030 that takes effect July 1, 2025 (as already amended by 2023 c 77 to add a tribal police department officer category), inserting it as a new subsection so both changes coexist.

Section 3 (the July 2024 version of the amendment) expires July 1, 2025, and Section 4 (the tribal-officer-compatible version) takes effect July 1, 2025, sequencing the two amendments to the same subsection so there is no gap or conflict in coverage.

deep_whoAffected: Part-time (less-than-full-time), fully compensated general and limited authority Washington peace officers and law enforcement officers, who newly qualify for peace-officer status statewide and for LEOFF Plan 2 membership; full-time officers and existing bargaining units are protected from displacement.
deep_poi: Uses a dual-track (expire/effective) amendment pair on the same RCW 41.26.030 subsection to sequence this change against the already-enacted 2023 c 77 tribal-officer provision, a standard but easy-to-miss WA drafting mechanic that can obscure which version of the definition is live at a given date.

Pure eligibility/definitional expansion: no change to contribution rates, benefit multiplier, COLA, vesting, or funding policy; cost impact depends entirely on how many employers voluntarily adopt flexible work policies under the new chapter 49.28 section, since adoption is permissive ("may"), not mandatory.

Existing LEOFF service-credit thresholds (90/70-hour full, half, and quarter service-credit months) already accommodate part-time work, so no new crediting mechanism was needed, but final average salary for Plan 2 is based on the highest 60 consecutive service-credit months, meaning a late-career shift to part-time schedule would generally lower, not spike, a member's benefit.

The RCW 10.93.020 change reaches beyond LEOFF and pension eligibility into the general peace-officer certification and mutual-aid framework, conferring statewide peace-officer authority on part-time officers, not just retirement-system membership.
deep_oneLine: ESSB 5424 authorizes law enforcement agencies to adopt flexible/part-time work policies and, via a dual-track technical amendment sequenced against a companion tribal-officer provision, extends LEOFF Plan 2 membership and statewide peace-officer status to less-than-full-time commissioned officers beginning July 1, 2024.

brief: Concerning industrial insurance coverage for posttraumatic stress disorders affecting registered nurses.
triage_how: The bill extends workers' compensation coverage for posttraumatic stress disorder to registered nurses but does not affect pension systems or retirement benefits.

brief: Ensuring that firefighters who accept promotional firefighter positions within a fire department remain members of the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system.
haiku_summary: The bill expands LEOFF membership eligibility to include firefighters serving in positions that require an experienced firefighter, ensuring promoted firefighters remain in the system.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds new RCW 41.26.030(17)(d), defining 'firefighter' to include any person serving full time, fully compensated, as an employee of a fire department in a position that requires an experienced firefighter, so that a firefighter promoted into such a position keeps LEOFF membership instead of falling outside the statutory definition.

Relabels existing subsections (17)(d) through (h) as (e) through (i) to accommodate the new (d), including the carve-out for executive secretaries of fire protection district associations, which continues to state it does not apply to plan 2 members.
Corrects an internal cross-reference from RCW 18.73.030(12) to RCW 18.73.030(13) in the EMT-firefighter clause, conforming to a 2022 renumbering of that statute noted by the code reviser.

deep_whoAffected: Firefighters promoted into full-time positions within a fire department that require firefighting experience (e.g., fire marshal, training officer, inspector roles) but lack a distinct civil service firefighter exam, who gain continued/clarified LEOFF membership rather than risking exclusion from the definition of 'firefighter.'
deep_poi: The new (17)(d) standard - 'a position that requires an experienced firefighter' - is undefined and less concrete than the criteria used elsewhere in the same definition (civil service exam, named dispatcher/EMT certification requirements), leaving the employer or DRS to determine case by case which promotional positions qualify.

Unlike the neighboring carve-outs in (17)(e) and (17)(f), which expressly state they do not apply to plan 2 members, the new (17)(d) contains no such limitation, so on its face it extends to both plan 1 and plan 2, which broadens the fiscal exposure beyond a plan 1-only fix.

Because LEOFF is a closed, more generous system relative to PERS for local government employees, retaining promoted firefighters in LEOFF rather than letting them default into PERS has an actuarial cost and would ordinarily warrant a fiscal note from the state actuary given the membership-eligibility expansion.

The bill piggybacks an unrelated technical citation fix (18.73.030 renumbering) onto the same amendatory section as the substantive membership change, which is common drafting practice in RCW 41.26.030 but obscures the size of the substantive change within a large omnibus definitions section.
deep_oneLine: SB 5468 amends the LEOFF definitions statute, RCW 41.26.030, to add promotional (non-civil-service-tested) full-time firefighter positions requiring firefighting experience to the definition of 'firefighter,' keeping members who are promoted within a fire department in LEOFF rather than losing that status, and separately fixes a stale internal citation.

hidden_how: All 24 pension-term hits come from two copies of one long boilerplate sentence (RCW-style treasury investment-income allocation list) enumerating every state account/fund by name, including retirement and deferred-compensation accounts that already exist in law; the bill's only edit within that list is inserting "the covenant homeownership program account" into the enumeration so the new account earns pooled treasury interest like the others, with no retirement-system policy content.

hidden_passages.where: Lines 134 and 280 (two near-identical occurrences of the same enumerated-accounts sentence, likely original section and reenacted/amended section)
hidden_passages.what: A single run-on sentence listing over 100 state accounts and funds — including the deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts, department of retirement systems expense account, judges'/judicial retirement accounts, pension funding stabilization account, PERS plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, TRS plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, Washington public safety employees' plan 2 retirement account, school employees' retirement system combined plan 2/3 account, state patrol retirement account, volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, money-purchase retirement savings accounts, higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund, supplemental pension account, and Washington judicial retirement system account — that share in treasury pooled investment earnings based on average daily balance. These retirement/pension accounts are named only because they are pre-existing entries in this master list; the bill does not modify their terms.

hidden_passages.where: Lines 134 and 280, within the same sentence (marked with <TextRun amendingStyle="add">)
hidden_passages.what: The bill's actual operative amendment inserts "the covenant homeownership program account" into this list, so the newly created covenant homeownership account becomes entitled to its proportionate share of state treasury investment earnings, consistent with every other account already on the list (including the retirement accounts).

hidden_poi: The 24 pension-term hits are an artifact of one boilerplate account-enumeration clause (appears twice in the file) rather than distinct pension provisions scattered through the bill.
No contribution rates, benefit formulas, actuarial assumptions, or plan eligibility rules are touched anywhere in the text.

The bill's only substantive act relevant to this list is adding the new covenant homeownership program account so it can earn pooled treasury interest — the same mechanical treatment every other listed account (including PERS/TRS/LEOFF/deferred comp accounts) already receives.

This is a standard technical amendment pattern in WA budget/appropriations-adjacent bills: any time a new state account is created, its name is added to this same long RCW 43.79A.040-style list, which is why LEOFF, PERS, TRS, and deferred compensation terms show up as false positives in RCW-classification pension screens.
No pension provisos, contribution rate suspensions, or fiscal maneuvers touching retirement funds are present in this bill.

brief: Concerning health care coverage for retired or disabled employees denied coverage for failure to timely notify the authority of their intent
triage_how: The bill provides a remedial health insurance enrollment opportunity for retired employees from pension systems but does not amend any pension system benefits or rules.

hidden_how: Grepped for pension terms, found all 24 hits cluster inside two near-duplicate RCW 43.84.092 amendments (Sec. 9 and Sec. 10, pre/post July 1 2024 versions) that list dozens of state treasury accounts for investment-earnings allocation, then read lines 129-275 and 275-417 to confirm the only substantive change is insertion of "the covenant homeownership account" into that list.

hidden_passages.where: Lines 129-273 (Sec. 9, amending RCW 43.84.092, version effective until July 1, 2024) and lines 275-416 (Sec. 10, amending RCW 43.84.092, version effective July 1, 2024)
hidden_passages.what: Each section amends the treasury surplus-investment-earnings distribution statute by inserting a single new entry, 'the covenant homeownership account,' into a long pre-existing alphabetical list of ~140 state accounts and funds that receive a proportionate share of daily interest earnings. The list happens to include numerous retirement-related accounts (PERS plan 1 account, PERS combined plan 2/3 account, TRS plan 1 account, TRS combined plan 2/3 account, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, Washington school employees' retirement system combined plan 2/3 account, Washington state patrol retirement account, judges' retirement account, judicial retirement administrative/principal accounts, deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts, money-purchase retirement savings administrative/principal accounts, department of retirement systems expense account, pension funding stabilization account, supplemental pension account, higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund, volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, Washington public safety employees' plan 2 retirement account, Washington judicial retirement system account). None of these accounts' treatment, funding rules, or interest-crediting mechanics are altered; they are simply carried-forward text from the existing statute, duplicated because the statute has two effective-date versions.

hidden_poi: All 24 pension-term hits come from just two near-duplicate statutory blocks (Sec. 9 and Sec. 10), both amendments to RCW 43.84.092, the general treasury investment-earnings-crediting statute -- not a pension statute.

The bill's only edit to those two sections is adding 'the covenant homeownership account' to the existing account list; no dollar amounts, rates, formulas, or eligibility rules for any retirement account are touched.

Sec. 9 expires July 1, 2024 and Sec. 10 takes effect July 1, 2024 -- standard technique for amending a statute that already has scheduled dual versions; unrelated to pensions, just means the same boilerplate list appears twice in the bill text.
No provisions in this bill create, suspend, or adjust employer/employee contribution rates, actuarial assumptions, or benefit formulas for PERS/TRS/SERS/LEOFF/WSPRS or any other system.

This is a good illustration of why keyword-based pension-bill classifiers produce false positives: RCW 43.84.092's omnibus account list is a common vector for spurious pension-term hits any time a new state account is created and added to it.

brief: Concerning postretirement employment in nursing positions for a state agency.
haiku_summary: The bill allows retired public employees to work as licensed nurses for state agencies up to 1,040 hours per calendar year while receiving uninterrupted pension benefits through July 1, 2026.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (2)(b) to RCW 41.37.050 (PSERS) letting a retiree who has met the break-in-employment requirement and who takes a nonadministrative licensed-nurse position with a state agency keep receiving pension payments while working, until service exceeds 1,040 hours in a calendar year, effective from the act's effective date through July 1, 2026.

Adds new subsection (2)(c) to RCW 41.40.037 (PERS, plans 1/2/3, including alternate early retirees under RCW 41.40.630(3)(b) and 41.40.820(3)(b)) granting the identical nonadministrative licensed-nurse, state-agency, 1,040-hour, effective-date-to-July 1, 2026 carve-out from pension suspension.
New uncodified Section 3 declares the act necessary for immediate preservation of public peace, health, or safety and gives it an immediate effective date.

deep_whoAffected: Retired PSERS and PERS members (plans 1, 2, and 3, including alternate early retirees) who return to nonadministrative licensed-nursing positions with a state agency gain a temporary, higher (1,040-hour) postretirement work threshold before pension suspension; other retirees remain capped at 867 hours.
deep_poi: The carve-out is drawn extremely narrowly: nonadministrative, licensed-nurse, state-agency positions only, mirroring but distinct from the existing school-district nonadministrative-position carve-out already in RCW 41.40.037(2)(b) (which runs through July 1, 2025) — this bill effectively extends the same double-dipping relief mechanism to a new, unnamed 'state agency' population, almost certainly targeting DOC or DSHS institutional nursing shortages.

Raises the postretirement work ceiling from 867 hours (the standard limit in both sections' (2)(a)) to 1,040 hours for this class, a nontrivial expansion of allowable hours worked while drawing full pension, which increases double-dipping cost exposure to the retirement systems for the duration of the carve-out.

The sunset date (July 1, 2026) is set well past the bill's own emergency immediate-effective-date, giving roughly three years of carve-out life — long for what is framed as a stopgap staffing fix, and worth checking against any fiscal note for projected cost.

Emergency clause plus immediate effective date for what is otherwise a narrow personnel-policy tweak signals urgent, likely institution-specific staffing pressure (e.g., 24-hour nursing coverage at a state facility) rather than a broad systemic pension change.
deep_oneLine: SSB 5538 creates a temporary, sunsetting (through July 1, 2026) return-to-work carve-out in both PSERS and PERS letting retired licensed nurses working nonadministrative positions for a state agency draw full pension payments while working up to 1,040 hours a year, bypassing the usual 867-hour postretirement work cap, and takes effect immediately under an emergency clause.

triage_how: The bill splits the volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund into two separate accounts to comply with federal tax qualification requirements for qualified employee benefit plans.

hidden_how: All 24 pension-related term hits fall inside two boilerplate RCW 43.84.092 treasury income account distribution lists (Sections 14 and 15, the pre- and post-7/1/2024 versions of the same statute) that enumerate every state account entitled to a share of investment earnings, and the bill's only substantive change there is adding a new driver's education safety improvement account to that alphabetical list, not altering any retirement system's benefits, contributions, or funding mechanics.

hidden_passages.where: Lines 253-258 (Sec. 14, RCW 43.84.092, version effective until 7/1/2024) and lines 399-404 (Sec. 15, RCW 43.84.092, version effective 7/1/2024) - Deposit of surplus balance investment earnings, Treasury income account, Accounts and funds credited

No contribution rates, benefit formulas, actuarial assumptions, or DRS administrative authority are amended anywhere in this bill.

Sections 14 and 15 are near-duplicates (pre- and post-July 1, 2024 versions of the same RCW) which is why the pension account list, and thus the term count, appears twice, roughly doubling the raw occurrence count without adding substantive scope.

No appropriations provisos, contribution-rate suspensions, or other fiscal maneuvers touching retirement funds appear anywhere in the bill; this is a young-driver-licensing bill, and the pension references are a mechanical byproduct of amending an omnibus earnings-distribution statute.

brief: Concerning public employee retirees.
haiku_summary: The bill establishes an Office of Ombuds for Retiree Benefits within the Department of Retirement Systems to advocate for and investigate complaints from members and retirees of all department-administered systems.

deep_provisions.detail: Creates a governor-appointed office of the ombuds for retiree benefits within DRS, with a six-year term, removal only for cause, staffing capped at four for the first two years, defined qualifications, advocacy/complaint-resolution/referral duties, a toll-free line, confidentiality of records, good-faith immunity, whistleblower protection for DRS employees who cooperate, a dedicated assistant attorney general, and a required website link.
deep_provisions.cites: new sections added to chapter 41.50 RCW (Secs. 1-9, 12, 19)

deep_provisions.detail: Funds the ombuds office through the DRS expense fund (RCW 41.50.110) and the health care authority administrative account (RCW 41.05.130), i.e., through system/employer rate charges rather than a general fund appropriation.

Requires an annual ombuds report to the governor, the Select Committee on Pension Policy, and the LEOFF 2 board, describing issues handled, monitoring activity, and recommended remedial action, first due April 1, 2024.
Tolls a member's or retiree's time to file a notice of appeal under chapter 34.05 RCW while a matter is under ombuds investigation, until the ombuds decides and DRS responds.

Defines 'in the line of duty' for LEOFF/PSERS purposes to match 'in the course of employment' under the industrial insurance title, makes LEOFF 2 disability-retirement denials issued before the effective date subject to department review for line-of-duty status, and requires an occupational assessment whenever a disability denial rests on capacity for employment.
deep_provisions.cites: new section (Sec. 14); chapter 41.26 RCW; chapter 41.37 RCW; Title 51 RCW

deep_provisions.detail: Amends the DRS expense-fund statute to exclude the department's administrative fee and any employer unfunded-liability charge from the calculation of employer contributions charged to a member when purchasing service credit.

Sets a minimum 90-day notice-of-appeal deadline for DRS decisions, requires at least a 90-day toll when DRS requests supporting information, and allows refiling of any claim previously dismissed for untimely appeal after such an information request.

Treats survivor-election change requests made between June 11, 2020 and the date IRS approval is received as timely, with any resulting benefit change effective only prospectively upon federal approval.

Expands the LEOFF plan 2 'basic salary' definition to include holiday payments (in addition to overtime already counted) and sick or vacation leave used by the member, increasing the compensation base used to calculate final average salary and benefits; also corrects a cross-reference to RCW 18.73.030's renumbered subsection.

deep_whoAffected: DRS-administered system retirees and members generally gain an ombuds/appeal-rights channel; LEOFF plan 2 members and disability applicants (including those previously denied) gain expanded compensation counting and a retroactive disability-review right; PERS plan 1 members with pre-1998 survivor elections and post-2020 election-change requesters gain a curative timeliness fix; employers bear the ombuds funding cost through DRS expense-fund and HCA account charges.
deep_poi: Creates a standing governance body (the ombuds office) with confidentiality, immunity, and subpoena-adjacent investigatory features, funded entirely through system expense-fund and HCA administrative-account rate charges rather than a general fund appropriation - a durable cost embedded in employer billing rates rather than a one-time budget item.

Section 14 reopens LEOFF 2 disability denials issued before the bill's effective date for line-of-duty redetermination, and Section 16 lets previously dismissed appeals be refiled - both create open-ended retroactive liability and reprocessing exposure with no cost estimate or funding offset stated in the bill text itself.

Section 18's expansion of LEOFF 2 'basic salary' to include holiday pay and used sick/vacation leave raises the compensation base used for final average salary, a modest but real spiking-adjacent cost shift onto the plan since it increases benefit levels without an offsetting contribution-rate change in the bill.

Section 15 shifts a cost away from members purchasing service credit (excluding DRS admin fee and employer UAL charge from the purchase price) - a narrow but precedent-setting exclusion that could invite requests to exclude other administrative surcharges elsewhere in the DRS fee structure.
deep_oneLine: SB 5625 creates a DRS retiree ombuds office funded by system expense-fund/HCA fees, tolls and lengthens member appeal deadlines with retroactive reopening of dismissed claims, expands LEOFF 2 disability-review rights and the 'basic salary' definition used for benefits, and excludes DRS administrative/UAL fees from the cost of purchasing service credit.

hidden_passages.what: Boilerplate statutory list of ~150 state treasury accounts and funds that receive a proportionate share of treasury investment earnings each month. hidden_poi: All 24 pension-term hits trace to just two passages (Sec. 4 and Sec. 5), which are duplicate amendments of the same RCW 43.84.092 section -- a common WA legislative pattern where a bill and a companion/appropriations act both amend the same section, with a null-and-void or same-effective-date contingency; check the bill's later sections for a contingency/null-and-void clause tying Sec. 4 vs Sec. 5 to which companion bill passes.
No pension contribution rates, benefit formulas, actuarial assumptions, or funding methods are touched anywhere in this bill.

No pension-related appropriations provisos found; this is a vehicle-impound/indigency bill, not a budget or omnibus act.

Bottom line for classification purposes: this is a false positive for pension-bill flagging -- the RCW section it double-amends happens to enumerate retirement accounts as part of a much longer boilerplate list.

The bill's only operative change to that list is adding a newly created transportation account (the "JUDY transportation future funding program account") for interest-earnings distribution -- a routine, nonsubstantive correction consistent with the bill's stated purpose of cleaning up chapter 182, Laws of 2022 (transportation).

No contribution rate, benefit formula, actuarial valuation, or funding-method language for any retirement system (PERS, TRS, SERS, LEOFF, WSPRS, PSERS, JRS) is touched; this is purely an interest-earnings-allocation mechanic, not a pension policy provision.

General lesson for the classifier: statutes like RCW 43.84.092 that enumerate dozens of state accounts (many of them pension funds) will trigger pension-keyword hits on any bill that amends them for unrelated reasons (e.g., adding a new account name) -- these should be flagged as likely false positives for pension-policy screening unless the added/removed text itself touches a retirement account or benefit term.

No pension provisos, contribution-rate suspensions, benefit changes, or fiscal maneuvers touching retirement funds appear anywhere in this bill; the pension-account names are simply pre-existing line items in a list this bill's drafters were required to reproduce in full and re-enact to add one new account.

brief: Concerning the definition of veteran and restoring honor to veterans.
haiku_summary: Bill expands the definition of veteran for state retirement systems to include individuals with less-than-honorable discharges, allowing more service members to access military service credit and related retirement benefits.

deep_provisions.detail: Redefines "veteran" for purposes of RCW 41.16.220, 41.20.050, and 41.40.170 by replacing the honorable-discharge requirement with the new "qualifying discharge" standard.
Redefines the general-purpose "veteran" status (used for hiring credit, tuition, licensing, and dozens of other statutes) to substitute "qualifying discharge" for "honorable discharge."

Creates a new statewide "qualifying discharge" standard covering honorable, general-under-honorable, and other-than-honorable discharges tied to VA benefit eligibility, plus any discharge characterization resulting from sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.
Directs the department of veterans affairs to run an outreach program explaining the act's eligibility changes, beginning on the section's effective date.
Ties WWII-era veteran bar-admission eligibility to the RCW 41.04.007 veteran definition instead of an honorable/other-than-dishonorable service standard.
Repeals the disability-discharge bar-admission provision, superseded by the new qualifying-discharge standard.
Extends the post-discharge gambling-license renewal grace period to any qualifying discharge rather than only an honorable discharge.
Allows discretionary high school diplomas for wartime-service veterans using the qualifying-discharge standard instead of "honorably discharged member."

Substitutes qualifying discharge for honorable service in the 10-year-service resident-tuition classification, cross-references the new LGBTQ-discharge carve-out, and explicitly excludes bad conduct discharge and officer dismissal (along with dishonorable discharge) from residency eligibility.
Redefines "eligible veteran or national guard member" for tuition waivers and textbook stipends using the qualifying-discharge standard.
Applies the qualifying-discharge standard to the teacher conditional-scholarship/loan-repayment program's veteran definition.
Ties the veterans' hiring and promotional examination scoring credit to qualifying discharge rather than honorable discharge.

Substitutes qualifying discharge for the prior honorable/not-undesirable-bad-conduct-dishonorable test in the state civil service veterans' layoff-and-seniority credit rule (up to five years added to unbroken state service).
Extends the fire and police civil-service commissions' entrance-examination military credit (keyed to RCW 41.04.010) to any qualifying discharge.

Clarifies that firefighters' relief-and-pension credit for wartime military service (up to five years, purchased by member contribution) requires an honorably discharged veteran or an honorable physical-reasons discharge, and explicit service "during a period of war" -- retaining the pre-bill honorable-discharge standard rather than the act's new qualifying-discharge definition.

Applies the same honorable-discharge-plus-period-of-war standard (not the new qualifying-discharge definition) to police relief-and-pension credit for wartime military service, purchasable up to five years by member contribution.

Adds an explicit "period of war" requirement (RCW 41.04.005) to PERS military-leave service-credit purchases, extends eligibility to honorable physical-reasons discharges, and corrects an erroneous cross-reference from RCW 41.40.005 to RCW 41.04.005 governing service credit for members who become retirement-eligible while still serving; survivor and total-incapacitation service-credit provisions continue to require proof of honorable service/discharge and are not updated to the new qualifying-discharge standard.
Extends the professional-license moratorium and post-discharge renewal grace period (director of licensing, and secretary of health) to any qualifying discharge.
Ties the certified veteran-owned business ownership test to the RCW 41.04.007 veteran definition rather than a separately-stated honorable/medical-honorable standard.

Redefines armed forces, Pearl Harbor, Purple Heart, and veterans/military emblem license-plate eligibility, and driver's-license veteran designation, around the qualifying-discharge standard, with the license-plate provisions delayed to an April 1, 2025 effective date and the current armed-forces-plate section expiring the same date.

Broadens state veterans' home admission from "honorably discharged" veterans of the armed forces to veterans meeting RCW 41.04.007's discharge requirements or otherwise eligible for VA medical care, and widens the covered branch definition from "armed forces" to "uniformed services."
Repeals an obsolete 1919/1923 statute recording honorable discharges for Spanish-American War and World War I veterans.
Substitutes qualifying discharge for honorable discharge across the county veterans'-assistance-fund veteran definition's several subcategories.

Changes the veteran-employment campaign's "veteran" definition from "honorably discharged" to the RCW 41.04.007 definition, and similarly updates reduced-rate hunting/fishing license eligibility for disabled veterans.

Removes the requirement that a deceased veteran's DD-214 show "honorable conditions" for a surviving spouse's property-tax exemption claim, substituting proof of qualification under RCW 41.04.005 with added documentation paths for other-than-honorable decedents, and exempts the act from standard tax-preference automatic-expiration/JLARC review requirements.

deep_whoAffected: Washington veterans with other-than-honorable or general discharges -- particularly those discharged due to sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression, or otherwise eligible for VA monetary benefits -- gain broad state veteran-benefit eligibility, except that PERS and the legacy firefighters'/police pension military-service-credit-purchase statutes (RCW 41.16.220, 41.20.050, 41.40.170) retain the pre-bill honorable-discharge/period-of-war standard and are not extended to this newly eligible population.
deep_poi: The bill's stated purpose is to align state veteran benefits with federal VA eligibility and to remedy discriminatory discharges, but the three military-service-credit-purchase pension statutes (RCW 41.16.220 firefighters, RCW 41.20.050 police, RCW 41.40.170 PERS) are conspicuously not updated to the new "qualifying discharge" definition -- they keep "honorably discharged" (plus a narrow physical-discharge exception) and, for PERS, add an explicit "period of war" test. LGBTQ-discharged and OTH veterans become eligible for tuition, hiring credit, license renewal, and bar admission under the new standard, but not for purchasing military service credit in these three retirement systems.

Section 20(4)(b) fixes a longstanding scrivener's-type cross-reference error (RCW 41.40.005 corrected to RCW 41.04.005) in the PERS military-service-credit statute -- a pure technical correction bundled into an otherwise substantive bill.

Service-credit purchase under the three pension statutes remains member-funded (restoration of withdrawn contributions or payment of the contribution rate for the credited period), so there is no direct employer or state cost-shift from this bill; the effect is instead a mismatch between who counts as a "veteran" for general benefit administration and who can buy military service credit toward a pension.

The only hard contingent effective date in the bill (Secs. 37-38) applies to license-plate provisions, which take effect and cause the prior armed-forces-plate section to expire on the same date, April 1, 2025 -- creating a brief window where DOL's plate-eligibility standard lags every other agency's qualifying-discharge standard under the act.
deep_oneLine: SSB 5871 replaces Washington's honorable-discharge standard with a broader "qualifying discharge" definition across roughly 30 veteran-benefit statutes (tuition, hiring credit, licensing, bar admission, veterans' home admission, tax exemptions), but leaves the PERS and legacy firefighters'/police pension military-service-credit-purchase statutes on the old honorable-discharge/period-of-war standard.

brief: Concerning membership in the public employees' retirement system for certain part-time bus drivers employed full-time by the federal government.
haiku_summary: The bill excludes from PERS membership part-time bus drivers employed by public transportation benefit areas serving naval shipyards who are simultaneously employed full-time by the federal government.

deep_provisions.detail: Adds new subsection (23) excluding from PERS membership persons hired on or after the effective date who are employed by a public transportation benefit area (per RCW 36.57A.010) as part-time bus drivers serving naval shipyards, if simultaneously employed full-time by the federal government and contributing to the federal employees' retirement system.

Splits the strike-through reference to the 'volunteer firefighters' and reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund' into two separately named funds (the firefighters' fund and the reserve officers' fund) to conform subsection (4)(c) to a 2023 statutory fund split.
deep_provisions.cites: RCW 41.40.023(4)(c); conforms to 2023 c 73 s 6 amending RCW 41.24.030

deep_provisions.detail: Updates the reference to the liquor control board to the liquor and cannabis board in subsection (10), a technical rename already reflected in 2015 c 70 s 3.
Replaces the trailing conjunction after subsection (21) and adds 'and' after subsection (22) to grammatically accommodate the new subsection (23).

deep_whoAffected: A narrow class of newly hired part-time transit bus drivers who serve naval shipyard routes for a public transportation benefit area while also working full-time federal jobs under FERS; they are excluded from PERS membership, while current employees in that role before the effective date are unaffected.
deep_poi: The carve-out is defined by an unusually specific fact pattern (part-time PTBA bus driver, naval shipyard routes, simultaneous full-time federal employment under FERS) rather than by job classification alone, suggesting it targets a known, small, identifiable group of workers (likely near a specific shipyard such as PSNS in Bremerton) rather than a general policy class.

brief: Concerning interruptive military service credit for members of the state retirement systems.
haiku_summary: The bill expands eligibility for no-cost military service credit in state retirement systems by allowing members awarded military campaign, expeditionary, or service badges or medals to receive free service credit, replacing the prior requirement of service during a declared period of war.

deep_provisions.detail: Replaces the requirement that interruptive military service occur "during a period of war as defined in RCW 41.04.005" with a requirement that the member was awarded a campaign, expeditionary, or service badge or medal, as the alternate (no member-contribution) path to up to five years of free service credit for the member, for a deceased member's survivors, and for a disabled member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit for the member, surviving spouse/child, and totally incapacitated member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit for the member, surviving spouse/child, and totally incapacitated member.

Same substitution of the medal/badge criterion for the period-of-war criterion governing no-cost interruptive military service credit, applied to the WSPRS provisions for members commissioned on or after January 1, 2003, their survivors, and disabled members; leaves intact the separate pre-2003-commission provision allowing up to five years of credited uniformed service without regard to whether the member left Patrol employment to serve.

New uncodified section makes the expanded no-cost military service credit eligibility retroactive for all RCW 41.50.030 retirement systems and requires the department to recalculate retirement benefits and adjust contributions for members who retired before the act's effective date if they have eligible military service.

deep_whoAffected: Members of LEOFF 2, PERS 2/3, PSERS 2, SERS 2/3, TRS 2/3, and WSPRS (post-2003-commission) who performed interruptive military service and hold a campaign, expeditionary, or service medal but did not serve during a formally defined "period of war" gain no-cost service credit eligibility, as do their surviving spouses/domestic partners/children and members who became totally incapacitated during such service; already-retired members with qualifying service gain retroactive benefit recalculation.
deep_poi: Section 7 requires DRS to retroactively recalculate benefits and adjust contributions for members who already retired, an unusual and administratively heavy remedy for a pension bill that implies the department must identify and reprocess an unknown population of past retirements.

Swapping the "period of war" test (tied to statutorily enumerated war periods under RCW 41.04.005) for a medal/badge test is more easily documented via DD-214 but likely expands the eligible population to campaigns and operations never designated a "period of war" (e.g., certain peacetime deployments and campaign medals), broadening the no-cost credit pool without a corresponding member contribution.

Because the credit is "no-cost" to the member once medal/badge proof is furnished, the fiscal exposure lands on the employer and state contribution side (the department bills the employer/state under each system's funding statutes), so the eligibility expansion is a cost shift to employers/the state rather than a member-funded benefit.

The amendment is executed nearly word-for-word across six separate chapters/systems (LEOFF 2, TRS, SERS, PSERS, PERS, WSPRS), which is efficient drafting but means any actuarial or drafting error in the template propagates across all six systems simultaneously; the WSPRS section also preserves a distinct, older, narrower carve-out for members commissioned before January 1, 2003.
deep_oneLine: SB 6000 replaces the "period of war" test with a campaign, expeditionary, or service medal/badge test for no-cost interruptive military service credit across LEOFF 2, PERS, PSERS, SERS, TRS, and WSPRS, and applies the expanded eligibility retroactively, requiring DRS to recalculate benefits and contributions for members who already retired.

brief: Concerning the purchase of pension service credit for authorized leaves of absence.
haiku_summary: The bill permits LEOFF Plan 2 members to purchase service credit for authorized unpaid leaves of absence if they retire instead of returning to work.

brief: Concerning the suspension of inactive cannabis producer licenses.
triage_how: This bill concerns cannabis producer licensing and market regulation, not Washington public retirement systems or benefits.

brief: Concerning actuarial funding of pension systems.
haiku_summary: The bill extends the amortization period for funding benefit improvements in public employees' and teachers' retirement plan 1 from ten to fifteen years and establishes employer and member contribution rates for fiscal years 2025-2026.

brief: Providing a benefit increase to certain retirees of the public employees' retirement system plan 1 and the teachers' retirement system plan 1.
haiku_summary: The bill provides a three percent cost-of-living adjustment to Plan 1 retirees of the Teachers' Retirement System and Public Employees' Retirement System, effective July 1, 2025, with a maximum monthly increase of $110.

brief: Concerning participation in the public employees' retirement system judicial benefit multiplier program by commissioners of the supreme court and court of appeals.
haiku_summary: The bill extends eligibility for the PERS judicial benefit multiplier program to Supreme Court and Court of Appeals commissioners, allowing them to elect enhanced retirement benefits between January 2026 and April 2026.

brief: Removing qualifiers related to the presumption of occupational disease for heart problems.
triage_how: The bill removes time qualifiers from occupational disease presumptions in workers' compensation law for firefighters and law enforcement, expanding eligibility for workers' comp benefits but not affecting pension systems, eligibility, or benefits.

brief: Repealing the long-term care services and supports trust program.
haiku_summary: The bill repeals the long-term care services and supports trust program, a state insurance program for home and community-based long-term care services.

brief: Providing additional plan choice to members of the teachers' retirement system plans 2 and 3, the school employees' retirement system plans 2 and 3, and the public employees' retirement systems plans 2 and 3.
haiku_summary: The bill grants members of the Teachers' Retirement System, School Employees' Retirement System, and Public Employees' Retirement System who did not receive plan choice at enrollment an irrevocable opportunity to transfer between plans.

brief: Ensuring access to state benefits and opportunities for veterans, uniformed service members, and military spouses.
haiku_summary: The bill expands eligibility for military service credit in public retirement systems to include members of the US Public Health Service commissioned corps and NOAA commissioned officer corps.

brief: Concerning workers' compensation benefits.
triage_how: It modifies workers' compensation benefit formulas based on family status but does not concern public retirement systems.

brief: Increasing defined benefit accrual for specified years of service in the state retirement systems.
haiku_summary: The bill adds one-half of one percent per service year to the defined benefit accrual for members' service years beyond 30 years in PERS, SERS, and TRS.

brief: Enabling county auditors and county treasurers to have designees appointed to firefighters' pension boards.
triage_how: The bill amends RCW 41.18 to enable county auditors and treasurers to appoint designees to firefighters' pension boards, directly modifying the governance structure of the fire protection district firefighters' pension system.

brief: Enhancing crisis response services through co-response integration and support.
triage_how: The bill establishes and supports co-response crisis services for behavioral health emergencies but does not amend retirement system law or substantively affect public retirement systems or benefits.

brief: Adopting the department of social and health services report recommendations addressing a regulatory oversight plan for continuing care reti
triage_how: The bill regulates private continuing care retirement communities and resident protections, not Washington public retirement systems or pension benefits.

brief: Extending the expiration of certain school employee postretirement employment restrictions.
haiku_summary: The bill extends to July 1, 2027 the period during which school employee retirees in certain positions may work in school districts and continue receiving pension benefits.

brief: Permitting individuals retired from the public employees' retirement system, the teachers' retirement system, and the school employees' retirement system additional opportunities to work for up to 1,040 hours per year while in receipt of pension benefits.
haiku_summary: The bill extends through July 1, 2029 a temporary provision allowing retirees from PERS, TRS, and SERS to work up to 1,040 hours annually in school-based positions while receiving full pension benefits.

brief: Concerning termination and restatement of plan 1 of the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system.
haiku_summary: The bill terminates LEOFF Plan 1 effective June 30, 2029, and establishes a restated system to administer remaining benefits for existing members and beneficiaries, with actuarially sufficient assets transferred to satisfy all plan liabilities.

brief: Allowing the Interstate 5 bridge replacement project toll facility bond retirement account to receive its proportionate share of earnings.

brief: Concerning the threshold for payment of a lump sum retirement allowance in lieu of a monthly benefit.

brief: Concerning payment of expenses from the earnings of retirement system trust funds.

brief: Changing the legal title for physician assistants to physician associates.
triage_how: The bill changes nomenclature for a licensed health profession in professional licensing and health insurance statutes without affecting public retirement systems or pension benefits.

triage_how: The bill provides property tax exemptions for seniors and disabled persons including some retirees, but does not substantively concern Washington public retirement systems or benefits.

brief: Concerning medical insurance premium reimbursements for surviving spouses of line of duty deaths.
haiku_summary: The bill adds a requirement that surviving spouses and dependent children of LEOFF members killed in the course of employment receive reimbursement for health insurance premiums, including Medicare Part A and Part B.

brief: Including standby pay as basic salary in the law enforcement officers' and firefighters' retirement system plan 2.
haiku_summary: The bill includes standby pay as compensable time in the basic salary definition for LEOFF Plan 2, increasing the pension calculation base.

brief: Establishing a tax on millionaires.
haiku_summary: The bill imposes a 9.90% income tax on Washington residents earning at least $1 million annually and subjects pension income to this tax.

hidden_how: All 78 pension-term hits are pre-existing pension/retirement account names swept along in a six-times-repeated mechanical reenactment of the treasury interest-distribution statute (RCW 43.84.092) that this transportation bill must touch only to add unrelated transportation accounts to the same long account list; no pension rate, benefit, contribution, or funding rule is altered.

hidden_passages.where: Sections 1001-1006 (lines 640-1502), each amending/reenacting RCW 43.84.092, Caption 'Deposit of surplus balance investment earnings—Treasury income account—Accounts and funds credited'
hidden_passages.what: Six near-identical reenactments of the statute governing how interest earned on state treasury balances is distributed. Each version lists roughly 150 state accounts/funds entitled to a proportionate share of treasury interest earnings (rather than having it swept to the general fund), including about 13 pension/retirement accounts per version: department of retirement systems expense account, deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts, higher education retirement plan supplemental benefit fund, judges' retirement account, judicial retirement administrative/principal accounts, money-purchase retirement savings administrative/principal accounts, pension funding stabilization account, PERS plan 1 account, PERS combined plan 2/3 account, reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, supplemental pension account, TRS plan 1 account, TRS combined plan 2/3 account, volunteer firefighters' relief and pension principal fund, Washington judicial retirement system account, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, WSPRS retirement account, and the school employees' retirement combined plan 2/3 account. The six versions correspond to different contingent effective-date windows created because multiple other 2025 session laws (2025 c 417, c 399, c 359, c 299, c 228) separately amended the same RCW section and had to be reconciled. The only substantive additions in this bill (marked amendingStyle='add') are new transportation-related accounts: the I-5 bridge replacement project toll facility bond retirement account, the Sandy Williams connecting communities program account, the statewide school-based bicycle education grant program account, the intelligent speed assistance device revolving account, and the medicaid access program account. No pension account is added, removed, retitled, or otherwise changed; each pension account's entitlement to proportionate interest carries forward unchanged from current law.

hidden_poi: No contribution rate, benefit formula, actuarial assumption, or pension funding methodology is touched anywhere in the bill.

The six-fold repetition (Sections 1001-1006) reflects layered contingent effective dates from other 2025 acts amending RCW 43.84.092, not six substantive policy changes; diffing any one version against the others shows only non-pension additions (new transportation/toll/grant accounts).

This is a recognizable structural pattern: any bill that must amend RCW 43.84.092 (or similar omnibus account-list statutes) will trip a pension-term classifier because pension trust/expense accounts are permanent fixtures of that master list, regardless of the amending bill's actual subject. Useful case for tuning false positives in RCW-classification screening, since 'PERS,' 'LEOFF,' 'TRS,' 'pension funding stabilization account,' etc. appearing here signal administrative boilerplate, not pension policymaking.
No appropriations provisos, contribution-rate suspensions, or fiscal maneuvers touching retirement funds appear anywhere in this transportation bill.

hidden_how: Grepped all pension-related terms in the XML, found they cluster in six near-duplicate reenactments of RCW 43.84.092 (the treasury income account distribution list), read each in context, and confirmed the bill's only edit there is inserting one new non-pension account into that list.

hidden_passages.where: Lines 173-182 (Sec. 12), and near-duplicates at Sec. 13-17 around lines 356, 535, 698, 859, 1023
hidden_passages.what: SSB 6355 reenacts and amends RCW 43.84.092, the statute listing all state accounts/funds entitled to a proportionate share of state treasury investment earnings. That list, carried over unchanged, includes roughly a dozen retirement-related accounts: the department of retirement systems expense account, deferred compensation administrative/principal accounts, judges' retirement account, judicial retirement administrative/principal accounts, money-purchase retirement savings administrative/principal accounts, pension funding stabilization account, public employees' retirement system plan 1 account and combined plan 2/3 account, reserve officers' relief and pension principal fund, supplemental pension account, teachers' retirement system plan 1 and combined plan 2/3 accounts, volunteer firefighters' relief and pension principal fund, Washington judicial retirement system account, LEOFF plan 1 and plan 2 retirement accounts, Washington public safety employees' plan 2 retirement account, Washington school employees' retirement system combined plan 2/3 account, and Washington state patrol retirement account. This whole list appears six times because RCW 43.84.092 was independently amended by four other 2025 session laws plus this bill's contingent effective-date structure, requiring the reviser to reenact multiple parallel versions.

hidden_poi: The bill's only substantive edit to this section, in every one of the six copies, is adding a single new entry — 'the electric transmission capital account' — to the earnings-distribution list; this is consistent with the bill's stated subject (electric transmission system) and has nothing to do with pensions.

None of the pension/retirement account names, contribution mechanics, benefit formulas, or actuarial provisions are altered, added, or removed by this bill — they are pre-existing statutory text that rides along unchanged because the whole account list is reenacted verbatim.

The repetition (78 term hits across only 6 near-identical passages) is an artifact of Washington's reviser practice of publishing multiple contingent/effective-date versions of a section when several 2025 session laws amend the same RCW without reference to each other (see the Reviser's note at line 184), not a sign of hidden or scattered pension policy.
No occurrences of 'contribution rate', 'unfunded liability', 'COLA', 'benefit', or amendments to Title 41 RCW (the core pension title) appear anywhere in the bill.

Bottom line for an analyst: this is a clean 'not a pension bill' case — the RCW classifier's negative call is correct, and the term hits are pure boilerplate incidental to an omnibus account-list statute the bill happens to touch for an unrelated purpose.
